title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
body_text: Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere Skip to content calif .io Calif Research ↗ CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell Write once, RCE everywhere Story by the New York Times A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution. Begin ↓ Technical write-up ↘ Check your servers ↘ Recommendations ↘ The Story 01 Overview 02 Write once, RCE everywhere 03 Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! 04 Era of the centaur hacker 05 The tragedy of the commons 06 A call for vibe-uncoding After we disclosed PHP2Shell , we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java. Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL). While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language , powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies . It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems. Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single = : Copy AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by = . Write once, RCE everywhere Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs. Pre-auth RCE: Keycloak Atlassian Jira Atlassian Confluence JFrog Artifactory Jenkins PingFederate Post-auth RCE: Apache Kafka Broker Apache Solr Elasticsearch Gerrit Spinnaker The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own. Here are a demo video of the exploits running: Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! Yes. First time? Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life. To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted. Era of the centaur hacker As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker , part human, part AI. It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200. One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI. The tragedy of the commons Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it. Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk. Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place? A call for vibe-uncoding If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not. Earlier this year we found Squidbleed , an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed. Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains. This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford. The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding : identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface. With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?” The Write-up 01 The Tail of Base64 02 Discovery 03 The vulnerability 04 Exploitation strategy 05 Heap Feng Shui (Grooming) 06 Remote Heap Feng Shui 07 Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries 08 Limitations 09 PoC 10 Affected products 11 Recommendations 12 Credits The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. Lesson learned Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? Note That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way. The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ( '=' ) in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode): Copy // Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length) output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3 // handle padding if input[input_length - 1] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 if input[input_length - 2] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len) In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY= , or === , then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2 . Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64 , this results in output_mask == -1u64 . Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1 , the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64 , all 64 bytes are written during the following operation: Copy evmovdqub( Address(dest, dp) /* Address: destination address addr */, k1 /* k1 == output_mask */, tmp /* XMMRegister src register/value to write */, true, Assembler::AVX_512bit /* vector length */ ); The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid. At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding . When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ( [64 bytes] + '=' ) as input, that calculation allocates a 50 -byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub , so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48 , an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=' , because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher. Exploitation strategy The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable. We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to: Full controlled write to byte 0 (in bound) 4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound) Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes 48..63 , the value will always be 0x9a . The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length. We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer . Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write. If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader , from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens. From the writer and reader , the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution. But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage. Alternative strategy Other alignments conceptually exist (e.g. type confusion, registers control from GC itself). Due to time constraints, we have not researched them deeply, and this strategy generalized well enough for our cases. Give us a shout if you invent something new. Heap Feng Shui (Grooming) G1 divides the heap into fixed-size regions . Before the region arithmetic matters, the critical arrays have to leave their threads' private allocation ranges. HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB) , a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another. The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path . The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray. Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful. One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases. Remote Heap Feng Shui In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones. 01 / PARK THE REQUESTS PREFIX DELIVERED SHORT ENDING PARSER PADDING DELIVERED HELD WAITS WRITER DELIVERED HELD WAITS READER DELIVERED HELD WAITS DECODER DELIVERED HELD WAITS 02 / RELEASE THE SHORT ENDINGS PAD WRITER READER PAD DECODER CONTROLS ALLOCATION TIME G1 STILL CHOOSES THE ADDRESS The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces. The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target. Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again. WARM Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted. REHEARSE Optional safe round for calibration. TRIGGER Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer. DISCLOSE Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes. REPAIR Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path. FINISH Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request. Limitations Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default . Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade , later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them. Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot. PoC Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED : the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run. Copy import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Base64; /** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */ public final class Base64Trigger { private static volatile int sink; public static void main(String[] args) { Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder(); byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] target = new byte[4096]; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { sink += decoder.decode(valid, target); } Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a); boolean rejected = false; try { decoder.decode(malformed, target); } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) { rejected = true; } int changed = 0; int first = -1; int last = -1; for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) { if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) { changed++; if (first < 0) first = i; last = i; } } System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version")); System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name")); System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n", rejected, changed, first, last); if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) { System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED"); System.exit(1); } System.out.println("REPRODUCED"); } } We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later. Affected products Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer. Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable: Amazon Corretto Eclipse Temurin Microsoft Build of OpenJDK Azul Zulu BellSoft Liberica SAP SapMachine Red Hat OpenJDK Oracle OpenJDK Oracle Java SE Oracle GraalVM for JDK According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time. Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected. These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements: Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer On Linux, you can check whether your CPU is vulnerable with this command: Copy grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' The output must include all four flags. Recommendations OpenJDK released a security advisory and Oracle released a patch at 1:00pm PT on Nov 17, 2026. All Java users should update immediately. You can also mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with either: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM doesn't recognize it and will fail to start. Credits Research, write-up and exploits by Quang Luong. Exploit improvement by Jenish Rakholiya. Artwork by Michal Zalewski. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) was found and reported by Calif.io .   See also PHP2Shell and Squidbleed .

We published our anniversary launch release in print at Defcon 33, HOPE, WHY25 and some additional variations at several conferences around the world including AlligatorCon, B-Sides Canberra, Out of the Box, Datenspuren, DistrictCon, OffensiveCon, Recon, and Toorcamp. We included a CTF with exploit challenges and had puzzles and easter eggs included in the zine. We threw parties and had talks at Defcon and WHY25 to celebrate this milestone. More importantly, we got new research into people's hands. The point of the relaunch was to get people reading, researching, writing, and contributing again. We wanted the next person picking up Phrack to find something that made them sit down at a computer and start pulling a system apart. We owe a huge thanks to the authors, editors, artists, publishing partners, donors, and staff who made it happen. Writing the paper, working through revisions, putting the print editions together, paying the bills, and getting boxes of zines to the right places all take time and effort. Most of that work is invisible when you are holding the finished issue. We appreciate everyone who did it. And to the readers: thank you for giving a shit. Seeing someone get excited about an article, connect it to something they are working on, or realize that they could contribute something themselves makes the effort worthwhile. That exchange is how this thing keeps going. The relaunch worked, and this issue is the follow-through. --[ Present ] This is the third release curated by the new staff, and we are not slowing down. This issue is larger than last year's, with 23 main papers and eight additional articles in Line Noise. The subjects range from exploitation and reverse engineering to machine learning, hardware, and the history and culture that grew around this work. We have container escapes through the vDSO, use-after-free exploitation, QNX userland shellcode, Linux kernel research, and a Chromium renderer sandbox escape through Skia. Elsewhere, the issue takes on Windows smart card architecture, static taint analysis in Binary Ninja, and autonomous underwater vehicles. There is also work examining backdoors in machine learning and what it means to trust an AI system. One paper takes us from PhrackCTF to two WinFSP zero-days, which is a pretty good argument for continuing to put challenges in a zine. We also have four more articles in Phrack World History, including the story of the infamous SSH1 CRC32 vulnerability featured in The Matrix Reloaded as well as stories about blue boxing free phone calls, a confession of a hacker who tried to backdoor Linux kernel in 2003, and an early discovery of botnets for hire. Our Prophile features Halvar Flake, whose contributions to reverse engineering and security research are legendary. --[ Future ] In 2026, we find ourselves in a time of rapid technological change. It is hard to say what vulnerability research or red teaming will look like in another five years. AI has moved well beyond completing a line of code into agentic systems capable of analyzing source code and reverse engineering binaries to find and exploit vulnerabilities. We can be sure that the future will require us to continue to explore new ideas, create new tools, and push the boundaries of what is possible in the face of new challenges and opportunities created by the advancement of AI and automation systems. As the effort required to put ideas into practice falls, creativity and human intuition forged through experience is valued even higher. We hope that this release of Phrack will inspire new ideas, discussions, and collaborations that will keep the human side of hacking a critical element in shaping the future of technology and society. We will continue to do our part to support the community and provide a platform for sharing knowledge and ideas. We look forward to seeing what the future holds and we are excited to be a part of it. Read the papers, try the ideas, and challenge the conclusions. When you find something worth sharing, write it up and send it in. We have another issue to put together, and some of you should be in it! --[ Greetz ] To those who have supported us the past three years helping to restore vitality to Phrack, we thank you. Conferences who funded prints: Defcon, OffensiveCon, Recon, Unprompted[AU], Unprompted[US], BSides Canberra, Alligatorcon, TenguCon Sponsors & Major Donors - WatchTowr, Elltam, Verichains, BShield, TrustedSec, Binarly, Trenchant, Praetorian (WWSUL), EFF, Blaze, EMX, Mullvad, ToorCon, Hacker Initiative, Endrazine, Dug Song, Napster, halvar, Horizon, Huku, Julio Auto, Gadi, and the rest of the people who stepped up with smaller donations. Artists - Ian Dash, pinguino, tainted, pepper, mar, xer0, abstrakt, ToscaKaiser, h7, zir, Mick, p0rtL, netspooky, ackmage, digitalis, Tedsig42, and the many others who submitted their work for consideration. Reviewers - barbie, bsdaemon, C, chompie, danielcuthbert, devinc, grugq, joern, jordan9001, K3, richinseattle, roddux, saber, skyper, SSHad0w, TMZ, zh4ck All the authors past and present who are now bound to the history of phrack. The unnamed ones who have helped us with logistics and carrying literal tons of paper around conferences to deliver them into the hands of the next generation. --[ Disclaimer ] All information in Phrack Magazine is, to the best of the ability of the editors and contributors, truthful and accurate. When possible, all facts are checked, all code is compiled. However, we are not omniscient (hell, we don’t even get paid). It is entirely possible something contained within this publication is incorrect in some way. If this is the case, please drop us some email so that we can correct it in a future issue. Also, keep in mind that Phrack Magazine accepts no responsibility for the entirely stupid (or illegal) things people may do with the information contained herein. Phrack is a compendium of knowledge, wisdom, wit, and sass. We neither advocate, condone nor participate in any sort of illicit behavior. But we will sit back and watch. Lastly, it bears mentioning that the opinions that may be expressed in the articles of Phrack Magazine are intellectual property of their authors. title: 350 years ago, Ole Rømer discovered that light has a finite speed
body_text: 350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed Jump to main content Discover our other sites: Norske og internasjonale forskningsnyheter Forskningsnyheter for unge Science news from Norway in English Science news from Norway in English Meninger, debatt og blogger skrevet av forskere Meninger, debatt og blogger skrevet av forskere Forskning.nos stillingsmarked Health Society Environment Natural Sciences Researchers' Zone You might be looking for... Health Covid-19 Food Exercise Sleep Society Work Sexuality Children and youth School and education History Archeology Vikings Environment Climate change Green energy Pollution Natural Science Physics Space Animals Ocean Fish Researchers' Zone Opinion Share your science Advertise with us Learn to write Contact us About us Annonse 350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed Ole Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light takes time to travel. The Danish astronomer Ole Rømer was responsible for an important discovery in the history of science. (Image: Wikimedia Commons) Elise Kjørstad Elise Kjørstad Journalist Published 16 November 2026 - 00:01 In September 1676, Ole Rømer made a prediction to the members of the Académie des Sciences in Paris.  He said that on November 9, Io, one of Jupiter's moons, would emerge from the planet's shadow ten minutes later than expected.  Rømer was right. In doing so, he proved that light travels at a finite speed. This knowledge became crucial to how we understand the universe today.  Until then, people had believed that light travelled instantaneously from one place to another.  Annonse Most viewed In a box in the basement lay four girls who died in the 1300s, still wearing red mittens on their hands 350 years ago, this man discovered that light has a finite speed Archaeologists have opened a Viking Age ship burial. The most exciting discovery may lie beneath the ship How dirty and unhygienic were people in the Middle Ages? People with this personality trait are more prone to anxiety and depression Regularly disappears behind Jupiter  Ole Rømer was a Danish astronomer and physicist. In 1671, he travelled to Paris, where he spent ten years as a member of the scientific academy and an astronomer at the Paris Observatory, according to the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia .  In the years leading up to the discovery, Rømer and other astronomers had been closely observing Io, Jupiter's third-largest moon.  "Io regularly disappears behind Jupiter, and this regularity made it possible to use the moon as a clock," Jacob Wüsthoff Linder tells Science Norway. He is a professor at NTNU's Department of Physics. Such a precise ‘clock’ could be useful for navigation, among other things. Ole Eggers Bjælde, a curator at the Science Museums at Aarhus University, writes this in an article on the popular-science media outlet Videnskab.dk .  Rømer studied and recorded the exact times when Io disappeared into Jupiter’s shadow and when it emerged on the other side.  Discovered a pattern Bjælde explains that because Io orbits so close to Jupiter, only one of these events could be observed on any given night. In the days and months before Jupiter and Earth reached their closest point to each other, astronomers could observe the moon disappearing into Jupiter’s shadow.  In the period after Jupiter and Earth were closest to each other, they could see Io emerging from the shadow.  Rømer compiled detailed measurements of these events and eventually noticed a pattern.  Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Professor Jacob Wüsthoff Linder. (Photo: Geir Mogen) "Rømer noticed that the eclipses occurred slightly later than expected when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, and slightly earlier when Earth was moving towards Jupiter," says Linder. "He realised that this was because the light had to travel a longer or shorter distance." "Impressive" Annonse In 1676, he therefore predicted that on November 9, Io would emerge from Jupiter's shadow ten minutes later than expected.  He was correct. If light travelled instantaneously, Io should have appeared ten minutes earlier.  Rømer demonstrated that light does not travel infinitely fast, says Linder. The finding was published shortly afterwards, on December 7, in Journal des sçavans .  Rømer was not the first to suggest that light has a finite speed, but he is regarded as the first to demonstrate it with evidence. Other philosophers and scientists had previously theorised that light has a finite speed, including the Greek philosopher Empedocles, the Muslim scientists Ibn al-Haytham and Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, and the English philosopher and natural scientist Roger Bacon, according to Wikipedia . "How accurate was Rømer's estimate of the speed of light compared with what we know today?" "Not very accurate by modern standards, but impressive for 1676," says Linder. Rømer concluded that light took approximately 22 minutes to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit, says Linder. That corresponds to roughly 225,000 kilometres per second, whereas the correct value is around 300,000 kilometres per second. "So his estimate was about 25 per cent too low. What really mattered, however, was not the exact figure, but that he demonstrated that the speed of light was finite and could be measured," he says. An illustration from Ole Rømer's article from 1676. B represents Jupiter, with its shadow shown by shading. K, F, L, and G indicate different observation points along Earth's orbit as Io enters and emerges from the shadow. (Illustration: Ole Rømer) Gained support Was Rømer's finding quickly accepted by other scientists? "It was probably a gradual process, and there were critical voices at first. The head of the observatory where Rømer worked, for example, never fully accepted his explanation. Nevertheless, his findings received support fairly quickly from prominent scientific figures such as Huygens, and later Newton," says Linder. Christiaan Huygens was a Dutch mathematician and astronomer. He is known for developing the wave theory of light, among other things. "The decisive blow came with James Bradley's discovery of stellar aberration about 50 years later, which provided a completely independent and strong confirmation that light has a finite speed," says Linder. Stellar aberration is the phenomenon in which stars appear to shift slightly in the sky throughout the year because Earth moves around the Sun while light travels at a finite speed, the researcher explains.  Looking into the past "Rømer was the first to demonstrate that light actually takes time to travel. It was also the first time anyone had produced a reasonably realistic estimate of the speed of light," says Linder.  This became very important for astronomy.  "Because when we look out into space, we are actually seeing things as they were when the light began its journey towards us. The farther away something is, the farther back in time we are looking," he says.  This has been important for understanding how the universe has evolved.  ——— Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik Read the Norwegian version of this article on forskning.no Related content Did the universe begin at a single point, or has it always been infinite? new tab) Facebook (opens in a new tab) Article link Copy link Share MAI Code 2 and MAI Code 2 Flash : t wo new coding models built for the everyday enterprise coding tasks , delivering leading performance at a fraction of the cost of competing models. Performance and speed for everyday coding MAI Code 2 is at the frontier of price-performance for common enterprise coding tasks and excels in taking code to production, deep debugging, multi-file implementation, repo wide reasoning, and UI. It does all of this while also delivering changes code maintainers would merge, at a fraction of frontier cost. Meanwhile, MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume work such as code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. Production quality at less than half the price To deliver the best price-performance, we’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at 40% of the cost, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the cost. 1 MAI Code 2 is also tuned for producing great dashboards and visualizations, and excels at visual coding. In blind frontend app evaluations, reviewers preferred its results over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. 2 In addition, MAI Code 2 Flash offers comparable performance to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 6 5% and 20% of the cost, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks. 3   Beyond coding MAI Code 2 is also becoming the workhorse behind Microsoft products. From Code 2 Flash we further optimized a single model, MAI Work Flash, to serve multiple Microsoft products across M365 and Fabric IQ. Excel: Our model is on par for accuracy and token efficiency with GPT 6 Luna across key internal Excel customer-scenario benchmarks.  PowerPoint: On key production benchmark scenarios that measure frequent PowerPoint tasks, our model performs on par with GPT 6 Luna in both quality and token efficiency.  Word: Our model performs similar to GPT 6.1 sol (while being significantly smaller) on 5 key internal benchmarks using ~42% fewer input tokens per call than GPT6.1 Sol in production.  Teams: Our model beats GPT 6 Luna at tracking decisions, filling knowledge gaps, and adapting custom instructions using up to 28% fewer tokens on instruction following and tool calling.  FabricIQ: In offline evaluation runs our MAI model outperforms GPT-5.6-sol, GPT-6-astra, and Opus-5.5 at DAX query generation, the core capability behind “Chat with your Data” for Power BI semantic models.  Get started MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash are available in GitHub Copilot, and Code 2 Flash is in limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . Soon, we’ll be releasing it on Open Router, Vercel, Hermes, Open Code, and Kilo. Learn more about customizing MAI Code 2 on our Custom Models page. About these results Results reflect evaluations on specific coding tasks and configurations. Performance and cost comparisons vary by workload, model configuration, reasoning effort, and pricing assumptions. MAI Code 2 performance and price: All models were run at max reasoning effort. DeepSWE 1.1, TerminalBench 2.1 and SWE Atlas were run on MSBench (Microsoft’s internal eval platform) with the GitHub Copilot CLI without subagents. FrontierCode 1.1 scores and costs are from Artificial Analysis; MAI-Code-2 cost is shown at its 50% promotional price. Visual coding: Blind human side-by-side evaluations of MAI Code 2 and GPT-6 Sol across user interfaces, games, data visualizations, 3D scenes, and SVG graphics. The preference covers both aesthetics and functionality , and is annotated by a total of 258 annotator s . MAI Code 2 Flash performance and price: All models were run at max reasoning effort. DeepSWE 1.1, TerminalBench 2.1 and SWE Atlas were run on MSBench with the GitHub Copilot CLI without subagents. MAI-Code-2-Flash cost is shown at its 50% promotio nal price. Lillis , Sean Lyngaas , Davis Winkie , Zachary Cohen Updated Nov 17, 2026, 10:33 PM ET Published Nov 17, 2026, 10:31 AM ET Updated Nov 17, 2026, 10:33 PM ET PUBLISHED Nov 17, 2026, 10:31 AM ET The National Security Agency (NSA) headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 2010. Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images Federal agencies National security Digital security See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Follow The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail. Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. This story has been updated with additional information. Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting. CNN’s Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting. body_text: Solid 2.0 - The Long Hold | Solid Skip to main content solid 2.0 Learn Blog Community About Back to blog Solid 2.0 - The Long Hold Solid 2.0 reaches stable after five years: async in the reactive graph, server functions, diagnostics built for agents, and a smaller API. Ryan Carniato Â· November 16, 2026 Â· 8 min read 5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then. A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler. More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time. Today that solution reaches stable. Async Graph If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design. This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands: function Profile ( props ) { const user = createMemo (() => fetchUser (props.id)); return ( < Loading fallback = {<Skeleton />} > < h1 class = {{ stale : isPending (user) }} > { user ().name} </ h1 > </ Loading > ); } fetchUser(props.id)); return ( <Loading fallback={<Skeleton />}> <h1 class={{ stale: isPending(user) }}>{user().name}</h1> </Loading> );}"> This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth. SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below. import { live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions" ; const stockPrice = live ( async function* ( symbol : string ) { "use server" ; for await ( const tick of subscribe (symbol)) yield tick.price; }); // in your component const price = createMemo (() => stockPrice ()) stockPrice())"> This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability. Built to Be Written by Agents "But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in. Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong. In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix: [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] Reactive value read directly in an effect callback will not update. Move it into a tracking scope (JSX, a memo, or an effect's compute function). in <App> âº <Item> âº effect at http://localhost:5173/src/Item.tsx:12:19 [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] what it means and how to fix it: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/solid-js/diagnostics/strict-read-untracked [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] agent repair guide: node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#strict_read_untracked âº <Item> âº effectat http://localhost:5173/src/Item.tsx:12:19[STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] what it means and how to fix it: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/solid-js/diagnostics/strict-read-untracked[STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] agent repair guide: node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#strict_read_untracked"> These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime. This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds. We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX , both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring. One Framework for All I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive. Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another. We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability. And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use. Less is More Somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource , batch , startTransition , on , produce , createComputed , createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them. The equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect ) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe important in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer. // async cascading dropdown function App () { const states = createMemo (() => getStates ( "US" )); const [ selectedState , setState ] = createSignal (() => states ()[ 0 ]); const cities = createMemo (() => getCities ( selectedState ())); const [ selectedCity , setCity ] = createSignal (() => cities ()[ 0 ]); return ( < Loading fallback = {<p>Loading ...</ p > } > < select onChange = {(e) => setState (e.target.value)} > < For each = { states ()} > {(state) => <option>{state}</option>} </ For > </ select > { ' ' } < select disabled = { isPending ( cities )} onChange = {(e) => setCity (e.target.value)} > < For each = { cities ()} > {(city) => <option>{city}</option>} </ For > </ select > < p > Selection : { selectedCity ()}, { selectedState ()} </ p > </ Loading > ); } getStates("US")); const [selectedState, setState] = createSignal(() => states()[0]); const cities = createMemo(() => getCities(selectedState())); const [selectedCity, setCity] = createSignal(() => cities()[0]); return ( <Loading fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}> <select onChange={(e) => setState(e.target.value)}> <For each={states()}>{(state) => <option>{state}</option>}</For> </select>{' '} <select disabled={isPending(cities)} onChange={(e) => setCity(e.target.value)}> <For each={cities()}>{(city) => <option>{city}</option>}</For> </select> <p> Selection: {selectedCity()}, {selectedState()} </p> </Loading> );}"> When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI. The Road Here The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on new reactivity ideas . The real effort started in late 2024. We announced the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen. Then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them. So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more. But mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet. Terminal window npm create solid@latest Solid 2.0 is here. Let's build. The Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown( isPending ) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land. Release Solid 2.0 Share X Bluesky Reddit Older Async Solid - One Graph, Two Machines All posts solid Simple and performant reactivity for building user interfaces. title: What is the best harness for each model?
body_text: Introducing FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 â RUNTA Runta Resources Docs Blog Pricing About Careers Start free with $50 credit Resources Docs Blog Pricing About Careers Social Discord GitHub X LinkedIn All Blog Contents TL;DR Result Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 What We Tested Setup and Scoring Results by Model The Harness Changes the Cost Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less? Where the Cost Comes From What the Best-Value Harnesses Share Limitations and Future Work Conclusion Appendix: Reference Tables References Introducing FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 November 17, 2026 Â· 14 min read Â· Shilin Zhu agents harness evaluation benchmark harbor TL;DR We partnered with Baseten to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions: when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model? Previously, our v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3. V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses Ã 5 models Ã 62 tasks Ã 4 attempts, 76Ã the size of v1.0. Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience. Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3. Cost ranks moved far between models. By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3. Result Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%. Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points). Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 V1.0 ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another. V1.1 runs each harness with five models. What We Tested Harnesses. 18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the appendix gives their versions. Models. Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 ( zai-org/GLM-5.3 ), GLM Flash ( zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash ), DeepSeek ( deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ), Muse ( meta-models/muse-spark-open ) and Kimi-K3 ( moonshotai/Kimi-K3 ). Tasks. 62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours. Setup and Scoring Configuration and Runtime We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harnessâs default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort. Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial. Scoring Method Table 1. Methodology This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of our dashboard : Average cost per task: the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5). Cost per pass: the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7). We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate Ã· cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line. Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model. Results by Model Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63. How Sure Are These Results? We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%). The Harness Changes the Cost The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts: Model, 92.8%: the differences between the five models. Harness, 2.3%: the part of the effect of a harness that is the same with every model. Pair, 4.9%: the rest. It also contains noise, because each cell has one value. So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise. With the Model Fixed, the Harness Changes the Cost by 1.8 to 5.0 Times Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. âChanceâ is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one. The Cheapest Harness per Task Changes With the Model Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task) Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse. Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26. A Higher Cost Does Not Give a Higher Score Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from â0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one. Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less? No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are. Start tokens: the input tokens of the first agent-loop request: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the task. Tools: the tools that the first request offers. Cache hit rate and steps: the mean over the passed trials. A step is one entry of the agent trajectory. Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was â0.03 to +0.02 (p â¥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the appendix give the values. Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass. Table 4. Start tokens, tools, cache hit rate, steps and cost per pass of each harness This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Where the Cost Comes From Figure 8. Inference cost of each harness, by token type or by trial outcome This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. All costs are inference estimates at list prices. The pass rate of the harness on the model card has an outline. Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%. Tokens and the Cache The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9). Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens) This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. One pair shows the effect of the cache. Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task) read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost. Most of the Cost Goes to Trials That Do Not Pass 64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass : 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts. What the Best-Value Harnesses Share The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests. One shell tool does most of the work. By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Piâs default prompt has four tools and sends file searches to bash : selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])], addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find"); Each request only adds to the one before it. The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens: # Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd) request prompt tokens cached tokens 8 15,954 15,616 9 16,351 15,936 10 16,999 16,320 No subagents and almost no summaries. Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6): .map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10); The five also share a weakness. Failed runs end with a confident answer. About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete: # Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e) Agent: - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and cancellation-cleanup tests. Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2 AssertionError: assert 0 == 2 Trials that did not pass took 60% (Codex CLI) to 69% (Alma) of the cost of each harness. A check before the harness stops could save part of it, but we did not test this. Limitations and Future Work Open models, one provider. Closed models can give different results. The cache and the prices are those of Baseten, and another provider can change the cost ranks. We plan two next steps: Closed models. We will add closed models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon. Long-horizon work. We will study how a harness that runs continuously in the cloud improves itself during long work. Conclusion When you change the model, think about changing the harness too. Test the candidate harnesses with your model on a private dataset of your own tasks, large enough to see past the noise. The model sets most of the cost, and the harness is second. The model explains 92.8% of the variance of cost per task. With the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.9 to 4.9 times as much per pass as the cheapest (1.8 to 5.0 times per task), so compare the cost when you pick a harness. A higher cost does not buy a higher pass rate. For each model, the rank correlation of cost per task and pass rate was â0.39 to +0.22. Size does not predict cost. mini-SWE-agent, the smallest harness, was 19th of 22 by cost per task over all models. Most of the cost, 64.5%, went to runs that did not pass. With the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of the failed runs ended with a confident final answer, not at the time limit. With a cheap model that has a wide range of pass rates, pick a harness with a high pass rate. Pass rates varied by harness, from 54.0% to 69.0% with DeepSeek. But each pass rate has a 95% interval of about Â±10 points, so a gap of a few points is a tie. For harness developers: cut steps, not just prompt tokens. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate did not predict cost per pass. Steps did, because every step sends the whole context again. Appendix: Reference Tables Table 2. Harness configurations This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Table 3. Reward-hacked trials of each harness This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Table 5. Prompt and tools of each harness This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript.
