How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
body_text: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification / claude.dev Blog [ H ] HOME [ M ] MODS [ D ] DOCS [ T ] TERMINAL Try Claude Code [ H ] HOME [ M ] MODS [ D ] DOCS [ T ] TERMINAL Engineering How the Claude Code team thinks about verification How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. AUTHOR Addy Osmani CATEGORY Engineering PUBLISHED Nov 16, 2026 READING TIME 10 min How the Claude Code team thinks about verification TREE â Not all tests are created equal: 3 tests worth investing in â How the Claude Code team thinks about verification â Good tests, good results ââââââââââââââââââââââââââââ 00% 10 MIN READ SHARE X.com LinkedIn Email Copy URL Copy markdown On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. Thatâs because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claudeâs work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agentâs performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid. If your tests are flaky youâll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before youâve committed the changes. Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in. E2E tests If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to foolâeither the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you whatâs broken. FIG A A unit test may show âError: Timeout after 30 seconds,â but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of whatâs broken. While unit tests are faster and less flaky, itâs possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test donât understand the full task. With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like CDP , simulators, or API harnesses. The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the userâs point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results. Property tests: constraints that canât break A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail. You start by writing a statement you think canât fail and then use a test library ( fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise. There are many properties in virtually every software project like: Round-trip encoding : âif you encode X then decode it back, you get X.â This works for parsing and serialization as well. Invariants : Things that must always be true, like âaccount balance can never become negative.â Idempotency : Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once. Equivalence : Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code. Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that arenât created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification. Differential tests: the old system is the oracle Differential tests are particularly effective for large-scale migration use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed. The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. Youâll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old. HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic , but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work. Verification means running the change Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude. Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work. To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes. Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid. When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic. Failing tests require human attention Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human. Code owners write their own checks The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff. Reliability checks trigger on the diff We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is â--resume loads old transcripts.â When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts wonât have it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matchesâusually 3 to 10âso nobody has to memorize past outages. One reviewer, multiple rounds We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code. We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. Itâs cheaper and finds more. Changes can't modify their own checks If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes . The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify. The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing. The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite. Start a new gate in observe mode In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified. We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes. Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted. Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck â Claude Code isn't perfect. Test your checks on what actually matters The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean. This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post , we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system. They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance. In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit. Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing . The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug. Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs. Turn misses into rules In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR. The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md. Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why. Rules need cleaning up too. Test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so we tidy them up on a routine. GOOD TESTS, GOOD RESULTS Weâve found that giving your agent a way to verify its work with a strong feedback loop makes all the difference. Treat your verification layer like you would any other system. Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesnât happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running. Do that and your job shifts from reading every diff to defining what âdoneâ looks like and reviewing the evidence, which is what lets you run many Claudes at once. body_text: What is w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com? Jack.cab What is w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com? Don't test in production. Published 11/15/2026 Iâm normal . This means I have a backlink monitor for this website. By pure chance, I was showcasing this to a friend when, suddenly, I got a new backlink: Backlinks APP 11/12/26, 2:37 PM New backlinks detected 1 new backlink detected: Most Popular Webpages In cab — siterate.org 11/12/26, 2:37 PM I tap in, 1 forgetting that 90% of backlinks I get are spam, and maybe this one could log my IP or even contain the 3-day 2 exploit chain of doom. Iâm greeted with this: Popular Webpages In *.cab Webpage Rank 23win.cab 110100 airports.cab 124393 pdf.cab 393627 hitclub.cab 422929 7m.cab 457524 max79.cab 712444 keonhacai5.cab 775520 jack.cab 783052 vic88.cab 856609 taixiuonline.cab 874131 Previous Next I sent an early draft of this article to another friend , who happens to be Vietnamese, and he told me thereâs five casino spam sites ahead of me, which I already knew because Iâm Faviconese. I have the most popular personal website on .cab, 3 but thatâs probably because I have the only personal website on .cab. I try some other TLDs. Rebane has the #1 .horse, synth.download is the 11th .download, whatever. Popular Webpages In *.net Webpage Rank sourceforge.net 83 cpanel.net 87 researchgate.net 103 php.net 106 launchpad.net 109 bugs.launchpad.net 128 cloudfront.net 152 behance.net 196 slideshare.net 204 themeforest.net 333 threads.net 388 w*****s.net 432 azurewebsites.net 532 doubleclick.net 579 earthlink.net 626 Previous Next page Redacted? I hover over it and discover it goes to windows.net.siterate.org . 4 Figuring out the pattern of redactions is not the topic of this article. I try .com. Popular Webpages In *.com Webpage Rank google.com 1 facebook.com 2 youtube.com 3 instagram.com 4 linkedin.com 5 twitter.com 6 apple.com 7 w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com what the fuck 8 googletagmanager.com 9 microsoft.com 10 github.com 11 play.google.com 12 apps.apple.com 14 x.com 16 maps.google.com 21 Previous Next page What the fuck???? I visited this domain (two days after it was registered, more on that in a second) and Firefox gave me the error , dnsNotFound. To this day it doesnât resolve. I do a web search of âw2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.comâ and I see references to the Majestic Million , a name I havenât heard in ages. Sure enough, thatâs what siterate.org uses: Position Domain Referring Subnets Referring IPs 1 google.com 504,763 61 2,177,943 673 2 facebook.com 463,877 178 2,143,213 1,688 3 youtube.com 421,041 31 1,760,838 1,323 4 instagram.com 392,625 92 1,739,231 1,295 5 linkedin.com 353,504 27 1,372,621 976 6 twitter.com 352,472 168 1,352,034 1,413 7 apple.com 283,697 290 845,882 607 8 w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com 274,833 961 853,298 4,759 80 ailawandorder.com 72,898 34 154,976 66 The Majestic Million ranks domains based on the number of different subnets linking to them. 5 This domain is the fastest growing in the top 100. Another, maybe unrelated anomaly I saw is ailawandorder.com (registered in 2023) at rank 80, whose âAbout Usâ page says its CEO is serving as a Board Member at Majestic. This made me check rank 800 in case there was a pattern, and no, there isnât, thatâs nsw.gov.au. Before I got rate limited from Majestic, I opened Site Explorer, and it told me w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com has 241,085,378 nofollow backlinks and 6 follow backlinks split across 5,163,708 referring domains. Checking Ahrefs, I see just 53 backlinks ; they read like the ones Iâve been getting since The Article fell off. All the backlinks on Majestic are âfreshâ, which means in the last 120 days. In fact, the domain was bought (not by me ð) for the first time (according to Certificate Transparency) on November 11, after most of the backlinks. I found an AI-generated PR from 2 weeks ago referencing the domain, and Tranco has data from October 5. Majestic has indexed 1,267 pages on this domain and crawled 27. The site isnât on the Wayback Machine so I canât collect its pages. In the Anchor Text table, the link count adds up to nine. There isnât an âotherâ section. Are the remaining 240 million links images? No, they arenât, it says the links are 100% TextLinks. Then I downloaded Majestic Million myself and searched for the domain. There were six subdomains. 5721d0cd26c13f745e1b368a2b5dfb0c.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 157 c0e3930fedc480e093a7bcad1a83c8a8.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 424 8628e302afeb346d191342ca114df068.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 554 2b1774347fbd085c628179dd339ddd26.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 822 e62f444581ce540d3cf5ac627b37c501.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 1,111 56aa73e7edd6f4e1fd3975b8b03761c0.w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com, rank 36,933 For comparison, jack.cab, which youâve clearly heard of, is rank 804,163. What the fuck is going on? By the way, w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com is at rank 38 on Tranco, which was designed to protect against this but still uses Majestic data. Theories I could probably figure out whatâs happening here in 30 seconds by buying a Majestic subscription but Iâm lazy. Copyright trap : maybe itâs fake, injected into the list by Majestic so they can discover whoâs using their list. Could w2rt6byl5nf1opmc-a.com and ailawandorder.com be in the top 100 for this reason? Probably not, because if they cared, theyâd relicense the list away from CC-BY. Also, the domains are ranking higher in Majestic over time instead of staying static. Majestic got hacked , and the hackers for some reason decided to tamper with the DB like this. No. Are you stupid, are you dumb, are you Dario Amodei, are you all three â½ Some loophole/gaming the rankings : Maybe âsubnetsâ is counted in a stupid way for IPv6 . A bunch of hacked websites linking to the domain : Seems unlikely, considering Iâm unable to find a single backlink in the wild that wouldnât be there for say, my website, and Ahrefs only has 53 backlinks for this domain. Besides the corrections I made in the conversation, I wrapped it in a background, then manually added Discordâs .headerText { margin-inline-end: .25rem } , then changed the App tag from height: .9375em to height: 1.1em because it felt wrong. title: Squircles
body_text: Squircles - Linebender Linebender About Blog Wiki Squircles A squircle is a shape intermediate between a square and a circle. There is no single mathematical definition, rather there are a number of curves that fit this shape. All general squircles are parametrized, and can vary between circle and square. Loading the interactive tester… Superellipse The best known squircle is the superellipse, popularized by Piet Hein. Martin Gardner wrote a detailed narrative of its origin in a Scientific American column in 1977. The text is replicated in https://piethein.com/superellipse/ but that’s missing equations and figures. The superellipse has the formula $|x|^n + |y|^n = 1$ (we’ll use a unit radius for convenience). When $n=2$ it is a circle, and it approaches a square asymptotically as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Measurement There is no standard measurement for squircles. For superellipses, the exponent is the most common parameter. A good choice is the coordinates of the midpoint of the quadrant, assuming a unit radius; here $x$ and $y$ are equal. The conversion formula is simple and intuitive: $x = 0.5^{1/n}$. This measurement is called "gauge" in the interactive demo above, and is the primary parameter; with the exception of some unreachable regions of parameter space, it should be possible to compare different squircle variants with similar gauge. Flat-sided squircles There are two basic approaches to squircle creation. One is a single analytic curve, where curvature reaches zero at the poles, but is otherwise nonzero. The other is mixing straight line segments with corners. A significant advantage of the latter approach is that it can adapt to rectangles of arbitrary aspect ratio without distorting the corner shape. The Apple squircle shape Squircles received renewed attention when Apple changed the icon shape from rounded rectangle to their own squircle in iOS 7 in 2013. There were several blog posts to analyze and recreate the shape. An early analysis suggested that it was a superellipse of exponent 5, but when people extracted the Béziers and looked more closely, that was found to be inaccurate. Rather, it’s a flat-sided squircle. For the raw Bézier path data of the Apple shape, the best source is the PaintCode blog . This blog correctly points out some bugs in that logic, and also has some details on behavior for oval rather than square aspect ratios. The Apple shape has a number of flaws, including one extraneous straight line segment, and a lack of symmetry. However, those flaws are minor, and really only reveal themselves under close analysis. The Apple shape has no additional parameter, so its variation is controlled entirely by the length of the flat side. With no flat side, it has a gauge fixed at 0.809. An extremely detailed analysis of the Apple shape is in The Art of Continuous Corners . The Figma squircle Figma published a blog post, Desperately Seeking Squircles , with an analysis of the Apple squircle and their own approximation. It is influential because Figma is an important design tool, because their writeup was compelling, and because there are any number of open source implementations of it, mostly TypeScript/JavaScript. squircle-path-kit from msurguy figma-squircle from phamfoo corner-smoothing from sanalabs (uses figma-squircle) squircle-js from bring-shrubbery (uses figma-squircle) figma_squircle from aloisdeniel (Dart/Flutter) Lisse from JaceThings The Figma blog contains a plot of the Béziers comprising a cleaned up version of iOS 7 rounded rectangle, revealing three Bézier segments per quadrant. It fixes the straight-line segment and the asymmetry, so is not an exact match. The middle segment is very close to an arc. The other segments are more problematic. They have zero curvature at the endpoints, so are G2 continuous with flat sides, but there is a curvature discontinuity with the middle (arc) section, and their curvature profile is not especially smooth. A reasonable guess is that it was drawn by hand to be approximately smooth. Without a flat side, the Figma squircle is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.854. Gauges up to 1 are of course attainable by adding the flat side. Clothoid squircles The Figma blog suggests “smoothed curvature profiles” which have a piecewise linear relationship between arc length and curvature. It then goes on to approximate them with cubic Bézier segments, but their approximation has fairly significant curvature discontinuities when joining to the circular arc. The clothoid squircle is worth describing explicitly, as it has G2 continuity (as opposed to G1 for the Figma approximation). The behavior is generally similar to the Figma variant. Without a flat side, it is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.790. The box decorations corner-shape spec Squircles got a big boost as they’re now standardized in CSS, as the corner-shape property of the box decorations spec . These specify real superellipse corners, with additional tweaks and support for animation. The Chromium superellipse approximation While the CSS spec mandates the actual superellipse shape, practical implementations will generally use a Bézier approximation. A blog post, The corner cases of implementing CSS corner-shape in Blink , gives an efficient closed-form approximation, with two Bézier segments per quadrant. This formula, determined using symbolic regression, is parametrized, and handles exponents 2 and above well. It is exact for placing the midpoint (this is part of the formula), so is well calibrated in that regard. Apple-like behavior with the corner-shape spec The early analysis of the Apple squircle shape as being approximately an exponent 5 superellipse was based on coarse shape only and didn't take into account its flat side. A much better match to the Apple shape is attainable using a superellipse with exponent 3 and a corresponding flat side length to match the gauge. This has G2 continuity and a similar curvature profile. This illustration was made using the Chromium approximation, so it should match the browser. Here's the CSS to accomplish the "close to Apple" squircle shape. Note that the parameter to the superellipse() function is the base-2 log of the exponent, so the value for an exponent of 3 is 1.585. . icon { aspect-ratio: 1 ; border-radius: 46.2% ; corner-shape: superellipse( 1.585 ); } Continuity A superellipse of exponent $n$ has continuity $G(\lceil n \rceil - 1)$. This includes the flat-sided variants, as, for exponent > 2, the endpoint of the quadrant has zero curvature. A perfect circle (and indeed, any even integer exponent) without flat sides is of course the exception, as it has an infinitely high order of continuity. As a general observation, for visual smoothness, the shape should have G2 continuity. Of the variants discussed, only the clothoid and superellipse (for n > 2) have this property. The Chromium approximation comes close; it doesn't have zero curvature by construction when joining the flat part, but does at the corner join by symmetry (unlike the Figma approximation, which has an additional arc there). Other squircles Quite a number of other curves can be pressed into service as squircles if need be. The polynomial spiral (“spiro”) curve can do a reasonable flat-sided squircle with G2 continuity. See the “suitcase corners” section of Raph's thesis , figure 7.2. Conic sections (hyperbolas). These approximate a sharp corner but are only G1 continuous (if flat sided). Fernández-Guasti squircle, defined by $x^2 + y^2 - s^2x^2y^2 = 1$. This is used in engineering but likely not in graphic design. The Wikipedia page on squircles has a “periodic squircle” which has very similar behavior to the Fernández-Guasti one (they are visually near indistinguishable). Related topics The offset curve of a squircle is not a squircle, but (a) it’s close, and (b) concentric squircles might be visually just as appealing or more so; for example a slightly rounded inner corner might look better than a sharp one if the curvature exceeds the stroke half-width. The blurred rounded rectangle approximation is based on applying shading to a superellipse; each iso-line is in fact a superellipse. title: We don't need more apps, we need better open source
body_text: We don't need more apps. We need better open source. — Jordan Krueger Skip to content Jordan Krueger About Projects 2076 All projects Movement work StarBase 118 Personal tools Built with AI Tools for progressives Blog CampaignHelp (opens in a new tab) Subscribe About Projects 2076 All projects Movement work StarBase 118 Personal tools Built with AI Tools for progressives Blog CampaignHelp (opens in a new tab) Subscribe November 17, 2026 · 4 min read We don't need more apps. We need better open source. Self-hosting Open web AI Discussed on Hacker News ·  231 points ·  127 comments Read the discussion on Hacker News Discussed on r/foss ·  ·  Read the discussion on r/foss Every day, a dozen people post a new app they built with AI over a weekend: a habit tracker, a to-do list, another note-taking app. I’m glad! More people building things is one of the best parts of this moment. But far less of that energy goes into the open source software we already rely on. People call this new way of building “vibecoding.” I hate the name; it makes a real shift in who gets to write software sound like a joke. I’ll call it AI-assisted coding, and I think it could aim somewhere more useful. Free and open source software already does most of what my clients and I need. What it often can’t do is run well on a cheap server, install in one step, or stay up without forum threads at 11pm. Where I’m coming from I self-host a lot of my own stuff, and I help progressive nonprofits with their tech for a living. I run a Matrix server (Synapse, Element and a moderation bot) for a community with thousands of users. I also run apps on Coolify and Hetzner, keep my paperwork in Paperless-ngx, and own a Mac Mini that’s always one download from a full disk. The software is usually great. Running it is the hard part. Install guides assume you know five other tools. Upgrades break things. Apps eat 4GB of RAM to serve a handful of people. Error messages tell you nothing. My nonprofit clients would love to leave Big Tech for privacy, cost and owning their data. But the open source option usually needs a part-time sysadmin they don’t have, so they pay for the corporate tool. Four jobs worth your weekend Make it faster. uv took a job Python developers do every day, installing packages, and made it 8 to 10 times faster than pip in its makers’ benchmarks (up to 115 times with a warm cache). Find the slow part of something people already use, measure it, fix it. Make it easy to install. Too many apps need a database, a cache, a background worker, a reverse proxy and a long config file before you see a login screen. Aim for one command, sensible defaults and a setup that works the first time on a cheap server. Make it friendly to run. Installing happens once; running it happens every day after. Give it a simple admin screen, safe upgrades, built-in backups, errors that say what to do next, and an easy, secure way to manage logins and add admins. Make it lighter. If a tool runs happily on a $5 server, an old laptop or a Raspberry Pi, far more people can use it. Lighter software costs less to run and uses less energy. Why this matters A new to-do app usually helps the few people who find it. Making a tool millions already use 20% lighter helps all of them, every day. This is also the work that slides when maintainers are tired, and many are unpaid volunteers. We saw the risk in 2024. Someone spent years earning the trust of the worn-out solo maintainer of xz, a compression tool inside most Linux systems, then slipped a backdoor into it. I think this unglamorous work suits AI well: profiling slow code, writing tests that make big changes safe, testing installers, rewriting cryptic errors, writing the missing docs. It takes patience more than brilliance, plus a person who checks every line. It matters politically too. If organizations are going to own their data instead of renting it from a few giant companies, open source has to be something a 20-person nonprofit can run. I want AI’s gains shared widely. Better public tools that anyone can use, change and share are one way to get there. Don’t be a jerk about it Maintainers have already seen the wrong way. The curl project ended its bug bounty in January 2026 after a flood of fake, AI-generated security reports. By April, its lead developer wrote that the fakes were mostly gone and almost every report used AI, most of them very good. The new problem is volume. Even good work can bury a maintainer. So: Use the thing first and find what actually hurts. Talk to maintainers before writing code. Nobody wants a surprise 4,000-line pull request. Bring numbers. “Startup went from 40 seconds to 4, here’s how I measured it” beats “faster.” Keep changes small and tested. Say you used AI, and own the result. Stick around to fix what breaks. If they say no, help downstream with a better installer or setup guide, and keep it current. Pick one tool Pick one open source tool you use. Find the most annoying thing about installing or running it. Spend a weekend fixing it, with the people who maintain it. Then tell me about it. title: Why 3dfx 1 cards had such a washed out color output?
body_text: John Carmack on X: "Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later. It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the p… / X Post Log in Sign up Post Log in Sign up John Carmack on X: "Both NeXT and 3DFX tried to “do the right thing” with color spaces, and it wound up generally making them look worse than competing options. I didn’t really understand it properly until years later. It is natural to think that a pixel with a value of 1.0 is emitting twice the photons as a pixel with a value of 0.5, so you can do the obvious linear math to calculate partial pixel coverage, blending a foreground over a background, or interpolating between colors in a texture. If displays are “linear”, that is correct. NeXT and 3DFX were much closer to linear than other contemporary displays. NeXT had crossover from the deep graphics understanding at Pixar, and 3DFX had the SGI heritage. They did this intentionally. If you have 10+ bits per channel like the professional rendering systems, linear displays are The Right Thing. Unfortunately, NeXTStation Colors were 4 bits per channel and 3DFX was 5 or 6 bits per channel, and there… it was not the right thing. Human eyes aren’t linear intensity sensors. We mostly register relative changes in intensity, so we can tell the difference between 0.01 and 0.02 as a huge doubling, while 0.99 to 1.00 is almost imperceptible. This distribution of intensities is often referred to as the “gamma” of the display system, but the actual curves like sRGB are a bit more complicated. If you only have a small number of discrete pixel values, you definitely don’t want to spread them evenly from 0 to 1! If you do, you will have good precision in the brights, but very stark “intensity bands” in the dark colors. If everything was authored specifically for 3DFX, you would still have the fundamental problem with the dark bands, but more accurate blending and filtering. The problem was that artists made all of their textures in paint programs on conventional non-linear displays, so when they were drawn by 3DFX cards, they got the characteristic “washed out color” look. You can mathematically correct textures for differences in display gamma, but I didn’t really understand the issue back in the glQuake days, and we were so enthralled by the absolute performance of 3DFX that the color fidelity didn’t get as much attention as it should have. Even today, tons of games don’t properly handle gamma across their textures and render targets. High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges." High resolutions and 24 bit color masks most of it, but you still see it in some slight shimmerings in high contrast textures and edges. title: If an App Asks for Full Disk Access or System and App Protection Override
body_text: ﻿ If an app asks for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override on your Mac - Apple Support Apple Store Mac iPad iPhone Watch Vision AirPods Home Entertainment Accessories Support 0 + If an app asks for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override on your Mac Starting in macOS 27.3, when some apps ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, you have the option to choose only specific protected folders or apps for the app to access. This puts you in control of what data is accessible to the app. Why apps ask for these permissions Apps that might ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override include backup apps, disk cleaners, file indexers, security apps, and others. While some of these apps operate best when granted broader access, others may ask for the same level of access even when they don't need it. It's important to understand the risks of granting broad access to any app, so you can make informed decisions about your own data and privacy. When you give an app Full Disk Access instead of choosing only specific protected folders for it to access, it can bypass system protections and access all of the files on your Mac, including your messages, emails, photos and videos, data from other user accounts, and more. It can read, change, delete, and export this data without asking. When you give an app System & App Protection Override, you can choose specific apps for it to control. If you allow it to bypass system protections instead, it can fully control your Mac and apps, which allows it to access all of your data. It can also see every window and app, including ones in the background, and capture every keystroke. What you can do An app might ask you to give it access to all of the files on your Mac, or to let it control your Mac. When you turn on access for the app in Privacy & Security settings, depending on the app, your Mac prompts you to: Allow or not allow the app to have access. This option appears for some apps, such as backup apps that ask for Full Disk Access, and screen readers and voice control tools that ask for Accessibility. Choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead. This option appears for other apps that ask for Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override. It allows the app to access only what you choose, while system protections stay in place for the rest of your data. If your Mac prompts you to choose specific protected folders or apps To keep more of your data protected, choose specific protected folders or apps for the app to access instead of bypassing system protections. Choose specific protected folders or apps When your Mac prompts you, click Choose Folder or Choose Apps, then: Check the app's setup instructions for information about which protected folders or apps it needs. Choose only the protected folders or apps that it needs. For System & App Protection Override, choose whether the app needs to ask for your permission before it controls each app. Use the menu next to each app to choose Ask First or At Any Time. If you're not sure which protected folders or apps to choose, contact the app developer . To stay protected, wait until you're sure which folders or apps that the app needs before giving access. You can change which protected folders or apps that the app can access at any time. If you're certain that an app needs Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override Bypassing system protections might expose your personal information to an app that doesn't behave as you expect. An app with Full Disk Access can read, change, delete, and export all of the files on your Mac, and an app with System & App Protection Override can fully control your Mac and apps. If you're certain that the app is from a trustworthy source and needs this level of access, you can give it Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override permissions by clicking Bypass System Protections: Confirm each action that the app will be able to take: Full Disk Access: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; and Browse As You on Websites. System & App Protection Override: Read, Change, Delete, and Export All Your Data; View Hidden and Recently Deleted Photos; Browse As You on Websites; Control Your Mac, Apps, and Settings; and Monitor Everything You Do. If you're absolutely sure that you want to give the app Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override, click Turn On Full Disk Access or Allow System & App Protection Override, then enter your password and click Modify Settings. Change or remove an app's access You can review app permissions in Privacy & Security settings, and change or remove them at any time. From the Apple menu, choose System Settings. Click Privacy & Security in the sidebar, then click Files & Folders, Full Disk Access, or System & App Protection Override. Change an app's access: Remove an app's access: Select the app, then click the Remove button (−). If asked, enter your password, then click Modify Settings. Change which protected folders or apps an app can access: In Files & Folders or System & App Protection Override, click the Info button (i) next to the app, make your changes, then click Done. Limit an app with Full Disk Access or System & App Protection Override to specific protected folders or apps: Remove the app's access, then click the Add button (+) to add the app again. If your Mac prompts you, choose specific folders or apps. If you remove an app's access, the app might not work as expected. Published Date:   November 16, 2026 Helpful? On Call Supercomputing REG AD saas Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back Richard Speed Richard Speed MICROSOFT ECOSYSTEM REPORTER Published mon 16 Nov 2026 // 11:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal 3 hours ago Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI! 5 hours ago Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open 11 hours ago Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits 15 hours ago Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage 1 day ago Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." REG AD "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." REG AD The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.  It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over. REG AD "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons." Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action. By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled. However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation –  an update that reverted the defective change." At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update. A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control? The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ® outlook microsoft saas outage Make us preferred on Google REG AD Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal NSA, Apple add to a week of high-profile network outages, largely attributed to 'routine maintenance' GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs Nvidia unveils an HPC-optimized Rubin GPU to challenge AMD's 288 teraFLOPS MI430X The future of datacenters depends on behind-the-meter energy generation PARTNER CONTENT: PARTNER CONTENT: Hyperscalers and colos have distinct power strategies, but for both, securing flexible, fast power relies on self-generated solutions Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI! title: Interpreting claims that a theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean
body_text: “…and the proof is checked in Lean” | Xena Xena Mathematicians learning Lean by doing. Skip to content Home About Xena Student projects Installing Lean and mathlib Bluesky Useful links. ← A Modern Reorganization of Mathematics “…and the proof is checked in Lean” Posted on November 12, 2026 by xenaproject This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done. Introduction Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it. This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet). Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement? A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement. import Mathlib def FermatsLastTheorem : Prop := ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0 , so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”. The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib , because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups . The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib ). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it! It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper . And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result. Question 2: does the code compile? Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code. When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean , they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code. Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop. It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not. Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated? I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib , so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37 , and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37 ? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical , how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics, The one-line answer: lake comparator . You can read more about this answer here . But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof. Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel? This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter . Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid . A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel. One final remark Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf. Summary/conclusions “It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly. Because I have this feeling that digitising mathematics will be really important one day. Bookmark the permalink . ← A Modern Reorganization of Mathematics 9 Responses to “…and the proof is checked in Lean” coolio says: November 12, 2026 at 1:42 am “Because Lean now has many kernels […] at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level.” Could you say which kernel you’re talking about here, and maybe how this claim of formal verification should be understand? (is the verification in some other proof assistant? couldn’t there be a soundness bug in that?) Like Like Reply xenaproject says: November 12, 2026 at 8:17 am I think I’ll defer to the master and just point you to https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-with-verified-kernels/ Like Like Reply coolio says: November 12, 2026 at 1:48 pm Thanks, I’d seen that blog post, but as someone who doesn’t know much about Lean, it’s a bit hard to interpret, and I’m interested in why *you* find it reassuring. In particular a statement like “Con-leche is the first kernel for Lean written in Lean and proven consistent.” doesn’t on the face of it make a whole lotta sense. How is it not circular to use Lean to prove that a Lean kernel is consistent? If there was a soundness bug, it could be used to prove anything in Lean, in particular that con-leche was consistent, right? Maybe the idea is that the consistency proof can be manually verified to not contain anything “weird” (though it seems this proof was produced by Claude…) Like Like xenaproject says: November 12, 2026 at 10:02 pm I’m really sorry, you need to ask these questions elsewhere (e.g. on the Lean Zulip). I am by no means an expert in these matters, all I know is that people who are experts have thought hard about them. Like Like tchow8 says: November 18, 2026 at 2:12 am “How is it not circular to use Lean to prove that a Lean kernel is consistent?” The first thing to keep in mind is that there are never any absolute guarantees in this business. Things can always go wrong. The point is to analyze carefully the mechanisms by which something could go wrong, and assess the risk. In this case, the question is whether a Lean consistency proof of a Lean kernel increases our confidence that the Lean kernel really is consistent. Well, what could go wrong? First, the Lean kernel would need to be inconsistent. Then, the inconsistency would have to be used to falsely prove that the Lean kernel is consistent. All this is possible, but generally speaking, exploiting kernel bugs is a highly nontrivial business. The Collatz example required very careful engineering and a deliberate attempt to prove something false. If we assume good faith on the part of the author of con-leche, the consistency proof of con-leche, though AI-generated, was not produced by instructing the AI to produce a proof of a false statement by any means possible. Under these circumstances, it’s much more likely that the consistency statement is actually true and that the AI generated a correct proof. If you believe this, then the consistency proof is a big improvement over no proof at all. Like Like dorchard says: November 12, 2026 at 10:33 am A very nice summary- thanks. Randy Pollack had a lovely paper, from 1997, that is along similar lines and goes a bit more into philosophical side of things too. For anyone interested who hasn’t seen it, worth a read: https://www.brics.dk/RS/97/18/BRICS-RS-97-18.pdf It tickles me that its opening line is “Suppose I say “Here is a machine-checked proof of Fermat’s last theorem (FLT)”” What a time to be alive! Like Liked by 1 person Reply boltonbailey says: November 13, 2026 at 2:23 am Nice post! One of the features I liked about the AI-driven https://github.com/SamuelSchlesinger/complexitylib-v1 when I was contributing to it heavily a few months ago was that it separated off many files and directories by putting “Internal” in the path as a signal that these files were meant to contain proof material and not to be read by humans. This made it easier to focus on the other files, which contained most of the key definitions and claims. I think this was a good innovation and that there should be more experimentation with clearer ways to denote what material in a library is human-vetted and what is not. Like Like Reply Dan says: November 13, 2026 at 1:04 pm Curious, what do you use for sandboxing Lean? Do you just run it in a Virtual Machine, or is there a more refined solution? body_text: Introducing Frame | TRMNL About Blog Developers Integrations For Business Discover Login Sign up About Blog Developers Integrations For Business Discover Case Studies Login Sign up ← Back to all posts Introducing Frame November 16, 2026 image-lightbox#open keydown.enter->image-lightbox#open turbo:before-cache@document->image-lightbox#close"> tl;dr our 3rd release, a full color 31.5" ePaper display in a handmade wooden frame, is now available for pre-order. watch the short film: the 1st batch is just ~470 units and i intend to ship at least a few by the end of 2026. most deliveries will happen early 2027. see logistics for more details or pre-order here . background in 2013 i founded ArtSpot. our vision was to give New Yorkers a bit of joy by exposing them to local art. we did this through informal agreements with dozens of cafes, small galleries, and restaurants. " let us curate art on your walls, get paid if someone buys it. " and it worked. sort of. finding artists was easy, building the platform was easy. getting permission from venues was slow but straightforward. the problem was nobody actually bought the art. i remember the admin email notification that first time a piece was sold. it was a small painting of Janelle Monáe. the buyer was my friend, a gift to me. here it is, still in my possession. anyway ArtSpot failed. five years later i paid back my investors (+ 13% interest). but the vision never went away. i love making and consuming art. opinionated platform i probably say " the most popular feature request since launch is ______ " too often. after saying no (and yes) to so many requests, it's tough to keep count. but with certainty, one of our strongest convictions was about color. TRMNL is not a television. it is not a clock. we avoid trying to do too much. then grayscale happened . photos look great. art is possible. community member Clark debuted Jaws (yes the movie), 1 frame at a time . 1-bit Jaws on TRMNL which got us thinking... maybe we were wrong about color. maybe it aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even bigger. introducing Frame today i'm thrilled to bury the lede and announce Frame . it's a 31.5 inch full color ePaper display, enclosed in a hand made wooden body that we manufacture ourselves. yes, we opened our own woodworking shop a few miles from HQ. a closer look at the workshop is coming soon. Schedule + Weather + Art in 1 screen Frame gets all the same features as other TRMNL devices, with a few additional perks spanning both the web platform and the hardware itself. watch the short film or read along below. Clock Sync often requested, always ignored, until now. Frame will update at specified moments of the day versus a relative "every N minutes" cadence. this reduces screen flicker while also extending the battery life and adding continuity to your schedule. Offline Mode the best interface is no interface the internet is cool but totally unnecessary. Frame's microSD port lets you run devices completely offline with zero personal information reaching our servers. Dedicated Power (optional) 1st port is available on the side panel like all TRMNL devices, a rechargeable battery is included (10-20k mAh available). but with Frame we added an extra USB-C port on the rear of the device, accessible with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity. Color Expertise Lazarus workbench some of my colleagues are snobs about ePaper dithering algorithms and LUTs (look-up tables). this is now your gain. over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display. it's also coming soon to our 4-color device , and yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure. Three Orientations Frame at Cafe Brûlée in LaGrange, Georgia Hang Frame in portrait or landscape orientation without additional hardware, both are built-in and flush mounted. You can optionally buy or build your own kickstand. And More we're negotiating with some of our favorite community developers to build more Frame-centric features. paying homage to ArtSpot , we just created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform. transparent supply chain before TRMNL i spent 10 years in b2b software and knew nothing about making physical products for everyday people. nobody ever blasted me on reddit about injection mold flow lines or damaged UPS packages. at best i'd get a G2 review every 3 months. this all changed in July 2024 and after shipping 60,000 devices to 79 countries we've gotten pickier about operational design. chief among these new requirements is doing as much production as possible in-house. here are Frame's components and where they're sourced: title: Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings
body_text: Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive - Groundwork Collaborative Menu Who We Are What We Do In The News Our Team Join Us Contact Us Gouged Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive November 16, 2026 Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events . The report, Deal or Decoy? Amazon’s Deceptive Discounts , examines products the retailer showcased as some the “best” discounts of the year to shoppers hunting for bargains during these sale events. A closer look at hundreds of these “deals” finds that Amazon frequently offered shoppers the same price, or in some cases a higher price, during recent holiday sale events than they could have paid just weeks earlier. The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale. During Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales in the past two years, prices for nearly 1 in 10 products advertised as “deals” were higher than what customers could have paid for the products in the month leading up to the sales. Groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025. These pages promote these deals as some of the “best” deals available. Amazon’s Black Friday 2025 deals page says, “With so many deals to explore, we’ve handpicked some of the best ones you’ll find.” Groundwork Collaborative President and CEO and report co-author Lindsay Owens , shared the following reaction: “Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Shoppers trust that the deals advertised to them deliver real savings because Amazon promotes them that way. But it turns out that these major sales aren’t all they’re cracked up to be. Instead, our investigation reveals that shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette. “Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars. With the holiday shopping season upon us and prices continuing to rise, shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. If Amazon can’t deliver that basic promise, lawmakers should hold them accountable.” Owens is the author of the recent book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet , which exposes how corporations are sophisticated pricing schemes to overcharge consumers. The report’s key findings include: The price of nearly 1 in 3 products that Amazon described as “deals” was the same – or higher – during sale events than what customers could have purchased them for in the month leading up to the sale. Some Amazon “deals” offered shoppers higher prices than they could have paid before the sale. On Black Friday 2025, a pair of yellow Hunter Women’s Short Rain Boots “on sale” for $126.99 had been $79.97 nine days before the sale event started, meaning customers looking for a deal could’ve paid 59% more if they waited for the sale. On Cyber Monday 2025, a pair of men’s UGG Butte boots “on sale” for $179.98 had been $98.40 roughly four weeks before the start of the sale event, meaning the “deal” cost 83% more than the recent low. Among these “worse” deals, the median sale-event price was 19% higher than what shoppers could have paid for the products in the weeks leading up to the sale. Since learning of our study, Amazon has removed the aforementioned deal pages our study drew from, but archived versions of these pages can be found at the following links: Black Friday 2024 , Cyber Monday 2024 , Black Friday 2025 , Cyber Monday 2025 . Amidst the ongoing affordability crisis, millions of Americans count on holiday sale events, like Black Friday, to deliver real savings. In 2025, a record 203 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, and this year, 70% of U.S. customers plan to take advantage of holiday promotions. Deal or Decoy calls on federal and state regulators to crack down on misleading discounts and require retailers to show the lowest price a product sold for in the previous 30 days when advertising a sale. ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND The new report builds on Groundwork’s work exposing corporate pricing abuses and delivering results for American consumers. In December 2025, Groundwork teamed up with Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union to expose how Instacart was charging shoppers different prices for the exact same groceries at the same store and time. The findings made national headlines , triggered investigations by the Federal Trade Commission and New York Attorney General , and prompted Instacart to end the practice just weeks later. Following the publication of Groundwork’s Owens’ book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet , the Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into major retailers’ use of customers’ personal data to set prices, adding to growing scrutiny of corporate pricing practices and their impact on Americans’ wallets in response to Groundwork and Owens’ research. In October 2026, Groundwork exposed Walmart’s creepy patent filings and pricing playbook. The report digs into patent filings, privacy disclosures, and technology investments to reveal how the retailer is building the infrastructure that could allow it to deploy personalized pricing at scale.
