title: Jiff 1.0: A datetime library for Rust
body_text: A datetime library for Rust - Andrew Gallant's Blog Andrew Gallant's Blog About Projects GitHub Sponsor Me A datetime library for Rust Nov 15, 2026 Jiff is a datetime library for Rust that encourages you to jump into the pit of success . Jiff automatically handles many common problems related to daylight saving time by putting time zone handling front and center into the API. Jiff has already seen widespread adoption in the Rust ecosystem. Jiff is pronounced like “gif” with a soft “g,” as in “gem.” This blog announces the Jiff 1.0 release by giving a tour of its API. Target audience : Rust programmers who need convenient datetime handling. Table of Contents The Jiff 1.0 Commitment Introduction Follow Along Terms The DateTime Onion Defining a time zone Durations When should I use Jiff? Parsing and Formatting FromStr and Display The “friendly” Duration Format strptime and strftime The jiff::fmt module Locale Sensitive Formatting via ICU4X Integration Date Manipulation Date Basics Date Arithmetic Date Rounding Other Calendars Which DateTime Type Do I Use? Span Manipulation Conclusion Motivation Inspiration The Jiff 1.0 Commitment Jiff is already used in production in many projects: uv, Cargo, Starship, fd, Nushell, mise, Jujutsu, uutils/coreutils and even as the basis for a Temporal implementation in AWS LLRT. It is time to call it 1.0. Unless some significant defect is found in Jiff’s API, my plan is to commit to Jiff 1.0 indefinitely. This is important because the intent is for Jiff to be an ecosystem building block that appears in the public API of other libraries. This makes Jiff an attractive public dependency, which means semver incompatible releases are likely to cause significant pain in the ecosystem. They will not be made lightly. To see a list of breaking changes between Jiff 0.2 and Jiff 1.0, please consult the CHANGELOG . Introduction In programming, a datetime library’s core functionality rests at the intersection of a computer system’s concept of time and a human’s concept of time. The prevailing notion of system time is Unix time . A human’s concept of time is far more complex, but the most popular such model is the Gregorian calendar coupled with either a 12-hour or 24-hour clock. At the core of every datetime library rests some routine for converting between these concepts. A datetime library typically provides much more than this. Indeed, datetime handling has historically been very difficult . My own belief is that the difficulty comes from poor modeling of the domain . Instead of encapsulating the complexity inside a reusable bundle of code, many datetime libraries pass some or all of the complexity on to its users. Jiff instead tries hard to encapsulate the complexity and make it difficult for users to do something wrong. ( Jiff is not the first to do this! ) In this section of the blog, we’ll do some very basic introductions. Follow Along To follow along with the examples in this blog, create a new Cargo project with dependencies on jiff and anyhow : mkdir jiff-playground cd jiff-playground cargo init --bin cargo add jiff anyhow $EDITOR src/main.rs Most examples are a complete self-contained Rust program. Just copy the code and replace whatever is in src/main.rs . Then run the program: cargo run Terms I am loath to present a dictionary. However, the datetime domain is littered with confusable terms, so I think it’s important to orient ourselves on a shared vocabulary. I’ve kept this section as small as possible. (Some terms, like “time zone,” are omitted here because they are best defined through exploration in the sections that follow.) Civil time : The time you see on your clock. And in general, the time that the humans in your approximate geographic vicinity also see. That is, civil time is a human coordinated agreement for communicating time in a particular geographic region. Civil time is also known as: local time, plain time, naive time, clock time and others. UTC : An abbreviation for Coordinated Universal Time ; it is a time standard that serves as the basis for civil time around the world. It was originally intended to roughly correspond to mean solar time . TAI : An abbreviation for International Atomic Time ; it is a time standard as measured by atomic clocks. It isn’t directly connected to mean solar time. Leap second : An adjustment to TAI to bring it closer to mean solar time and thus forming the basis of UTC. Unix time : UTC, but ignoring leap seconds. TAI and leap seconds won’t be a feature of this blog, but they are listed here in order to convey the difference between Unix time and UTC. The DateTime Onion As a way to transition into some of the core types of Jiff, I’ve come to think of its datetime types like an onion. In reverse order, we can build up its layers all the way to a ZonedDateTime . So let’s start with more terms, but this time, they are also types in Jiff: A civil::Date is a plain Gregorian date, unattached to any specific location. A civil::Time is a plain time on a clock, to nanosecond precision, unattached to any specific location. A civil::DateTime combines a civil::Date and a civil::Time to provide both a Gregorian date and a time on a clock. It is also unattached to any specific location. A Timestamp is an unambiguous specific instant in time regardless of geographic location, represented as the number of nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. A TimeZone is a set of rules for mapping a Timestamp to a civil::DateTime , and vice versa, in a specific geographic region. A ZonedDateTime combines a Timestamp , a civil::DateTime and a TimeZone to represent a specific instant in time in a specific geographic location. To make this a bit more concrete, we can see what this looks like in code. Since a time zone can map from a civil datetime to an instant in time, one way to create a zoned datetime requires only a civil datetime and a time zone: use jiff :: civil ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let date = civil :: date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ); let time = civil :: time ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); let datetime = date . to_datetime ( time ); // zdt is an initialism for "ZonedDateTime" let zdt = datetime . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . timestamp (). as_second (), 1793572200 ); Ok (()) } Another way to create a zoned datetime requires only a timestamp and a time zone. This is because time zones can also map a timestamp to a particular civil datetime: use jiff :: { civil , Timestamp }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let timestamp = Timestamp :: from_second ( 1793572200 ) ? ; let zdt = timestamp . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; // This is a shortcut for creating a civil datetime. // The previous example spells it out a bit more verbosely // for clarity. let expected = civil :: date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); assert_eq! ( zdt . datetime (), expected ); Ok (()) } Notice how we get the equivalent zoned datetime in both cases, but we come at it from different directions. In the first case, we start with a time that we might see on our clocks and calendars. In the second case, we start with a particular instant in time that we might get from a database or file system or some other system call. Defining a time zone There is one piece missing from the zoned datetime onion examples: the time zone offset . An offset represents the amount of time one must adjust UTC time in order to get civil time. For example, consider the time 2026-11-01T22:30:00 in UTC. In order to get the civil datetime for someone living in New York, one would subtract 5 hours: 2026-11-01T22:30:00 - 05:00 = 2026-11-01T17:30:00 Indeed, every zoned datetime has an offset associated with it: use jiff :: { civil , tz , Timestamp }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let timestamp = Timestamp :: from_second ( 1793572200 ) ? ; let zdt = timestamp . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (). seconds (), - ( 5 * 60 * 60 )); let dt = civil :: date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); let zdt = dt . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), tz :: offset ( - 5 )); Ok (()) } NOTE : The America/New_York string you see in the above example is an IANA Time Zone Database Identifier. The IANA Time Zone Database is a collection of time zone definitions that can be referenced by a short identifier string. Examples: Australia/Sydney , Asia/Tokyo , Europe/Berlin . When a civil datetime is combined with an offset, then what you get is always an instant in time. With the concept of an offset introduced, we can now give a more precise definition of a time zone. A time zone is a geographic region in which civil clocks agree and which provides the following: A mapping from an instant in time to an offset from UTC. The offset applied to an instant yields a civil datetime. A mapping from a civil datetime to a possibly ambiguous offset from UTC. The offset applied to a civil datetime yields an instant. Both mappings have been demonstrated in prior examples, but the mapping from civil datetime to an offset seems to be rather complicated due to some potential ambiguity. When does that ambiguity arise? An ambiguous offset occurs when the civil datetime either doesn’t correspond to a valid clock time in this time zone (e.g., when clocks are moved ahead for daylight saving time ) or where there could be multiple valid clock times (e.g., when clocks are moved backward for daylight saving time ). Let’s look at some examples. In this first example, we’ll take a look at times around the daylight saving time transition from summer time to standard time in New York. In New York, the clocks were “set back” by an hour at exactly 2AM. This caused the 1AM hour to repeat itself. use jiff :: { civil :: date , tz :: { offset , TimeZone }, }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let tz = TimeZone :: get ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; // During summer time, New York's offset from UTC is -04:00. let zdt = date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ). at ( 0 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). to_zoned_datetime ( tz . clone ()) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 4 )); // During standard time, New York's offset from UTC is -05:00. let zdt = date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ). at ( 2 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). to_zoned_datetime ( tz . clone ()) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 5 )); // But what does 01:30AM mean? Is it the first repetition or the second? // Jiff automatically chooses the first by default. let zdt = date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ). at ( 1 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). to_zoned_datetime ( tz . clone ()) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 4 )); Ok (()) } The above example shows how Jiff resolves the ambiguity when a “fold” occurs, or when there is a time zone transition that moves the civil time backwards. But we can actually dig down into lower level APIs to change how that ambiguity is resolved. By default, Jiff uses a “compatible” strategy that always selects the first repetition of a time in a fold. But other strategies can be selected by using APIs on a TimeZone directly: use jiff :: { civil :: date , tz :: { offset , TimeZone }, }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let tz = TimeZone :: get ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let dt = date ( 2026 , 11 , 1 ). at ( 1 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); // The same that Jiff uses by default. let zdt = tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ). compatible () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 4 )); // Always selects the earlier datetime. // For a fold, this is the same as the // default "compatible" strategy. let zdt = tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ). earlier () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 4 )); // Always selects the later datetime. // For a fold, this selects the second // occurrence of the 1AM hour! let zdt = tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ). later () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 5 )); // Always returns an error when there // is any ambiguity. assert_eq! ( tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ) . unambiguous () . unwrap_err () . to_string (), "error converting datetime to instant in time zone America/New_York: \ datetime is ambiguous \ since it falls into a fold between offsets -04 and -05" , ); Ok (()) } The same idea applies to gaps , or time zone transitions where there’s some civil time that gets skipped on civil clocks. For example, on March 8, 2026 at 2AM, civil time skipped ahead to 3AM: use jiff :: { civil :: date , tz :: { offset , TimeZone }, }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let tz = TimeZone :: get ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let dt = date ( 2026 , 3 , 8 ). at ( 2 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); // The "compatible" strategy selects // the later time in the case of gaps. let zdt = tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ). compatible () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 4 )); // Always selects the earlier datetime. // For a gap, this selects the hour // before the gap. let zdt = tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ). earlier () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 5 )); // Always selects the later datetime. // For a gap, this is the same as the // default "compatible" strategy. let zdt = tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ). later () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . offset (), offset ( - 4 )); // Always returns an error when there // is any ambiguity. assert_eq! ( tz . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( dt ) . unambiguous () . unwrap_err () . to_string (), "error converting datetime to instant in time zone America/New_York: \ datetime is ambiguous \ since it falls into a gap between offsets -05 and -04" , ); Ok (()) } Durations There are two remaining core types, both representing some notion of a duration: Span is a powerful hybrid duration that combines both calendar units (years, months, weeks, days) and physical time units (hours, minutes, seconds, milliseconds, microseconds, nanoseconds). It is a beefy type that preserves the individual unit values. SignedDuration is a signed version of std::time::Duration and always corresponds to a 96-bit integer number of nanoseconds. It can only represent physical time (units of hours or smaller) and not calendar units (units of days or greater). A Span is the preferred duration type to use whenever possible. Here’s a simple example that shows how to get the number of days between two civil dates: use jiff :: civil :: date ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d1 = date ( 2024 , 2 , 1 ); let d2 = date ( 2024 , 3 , 1 ); let span = d2 - d1 ; assert_eq! ( span . get_days (), 29 ); // or, equivalently: assert_eq! ( d1 . until ( d2 ) ? . get_days (), 29 ); // Flipping d1 and d2 gives the same result, // but negative. let span = d1 - d2 ; assert_eq! ( span . get_days (), - 29 ); Ok (()) } Durations can also be added to dates: use jiff :: { civil :: date , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d1 = date ( 2024 , 2 , 1 ); // This convenient syntax comes from the // `ToSpan` extension trait. let span = 29. days (); assert_eq! ( d1 . checked_add ( span ) ? , date ( 2024 , 3 , 1 )); Ok (()) } Generally speaking, whenever there is an operation involving a Span , there is an equivalent operation available with SignedDuration : use jiff :: { civil :: date , SignedDuration }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let dt1 = date ( 2024 , 2 , 1 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); let sdur = SignedDuration :: from_mins ( 90 ); assert_eq! ( dt1 . checked_add ( sdur ) ? , date ( 2024 , 2 , 1 ). at ( 19 , 0 , 0 , 0 )); Ok (()) } Notice that in the above example, we actually switched from using a civil::Date to a civil::DateTime . This was done to show how physical time units can be added. But note that the same can be accomplished with a Span , because it combines all units: use jiff :: { civil :: date , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let dt1 = date ( 2024 , 2 , 1 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ); let span = 1. hour (). minutes ( 30 ); assert_eq! ( dt1 . checked_add ( span ) ? , date ( 2024 , 2 , 1 ). at ( 19 , 0 , 0 , 0 )); // Calendar and physical time units can // be combined! let span = 1. month (). hours ( 1 ). minutes ( 30 ); assert_eq! ( dt1 . checked_add ( span ) ? , date ( 2024 , 3 , 1 ). at ( 19 , 0 , 0 , 0 )); Ok (()) } In brief, use a Span when you can. But when it’s too bulky or too slow, use a SignedDuration . One of the key benefits of a Span is that since it represents each unit value distinctly, one can preserve the original meaning of a duration. For example, it’s common to represent the runtime of films in minutes, even when the duration exceeds one hour. Indeed, a span of 2 hours is a distinct span from a span of 120 minutes: use jiff :: ToSpan ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span1 = 2. hours (); let span2 = 120. minutes (); // This means the spans are distinct values // in memory. assert_ne! ( span1 . fieldwise (), span2 . fieldwise ()); Ok (()) } The Span::fieldwise routine converts a Span into a value whose units can be compared in a field-by-field fashion. To compare spans based on the actual physical duration they represent, use Span::compare : let span1 = 2. hours (); let span2 = 120. minutes (); assert! ( span1 . compare ( span2 ) ? . is_eq ()); This was a very brief introduction to durations in Jiff. They are a lot more powerful than what is shown here. You might even try playing with the examples above to explore its nooks and crannies. We’ll cover their API in more detail in a later section. When should I use Jiff? Jiff isn’t always the right thing to use. Sometimes you can get by with something simpler. First and foremost, if you’re measuring the time something takes in a program, you should almost certainly be using monotonic time. This is available via std::time::Instant : use std :: time :: { Duration , Instant }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let start = Instant :: now (); // do some serious work std :: thread :: sleep ( Duration :: from_secs ( 1 )); let elapsed = Instant :: now (). duration_since ( start ); println! ( " {elapsed:?} " ); Ok (()) } If you do need to compute elapsed time using your system clock, then Jiff is very convenient for that: use std :: time :: Duration ; use jiff :: Timestamp ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { // assume `start` came from somewhere // over a network let start = Timestamp :: now (); std :: thread :: sleep ( Duration :: from_secs ( 1 )); let elapsed = Timestamp :: now (). duration_since ( start ); println! ( " {elapsed} " ); Ok (()) } But you don’t actually need Jiff for this. A std::time::SystemTime will work perfectly fine: use std :: time :: { Duration , SystemTime }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { // assume `start` came from somewhere // over a network let start = SystemTime :: now (); std :: thread :: sleep ( Duration :: from_secs ( 1 )); let elapsed = SystemTime :: now (). duration_since ( start ) ? ; println! ( " {elapsed:?} " ); Ok (()) } Where Jiff starts to become useful is when you need something beyond just an integer number of seconds since the Unix epoch. For example, some very hairy math is required in order to convert a SystemTime into an RFC 3339 timestamp like 2026-11-14T21:34:00Z . As long as you can live in UTC completely, don’t care about local time and can work with Unix timestamps only, then the Rust standard library won’t steer you wrong. Parsing and Formatting Conversion to and from strings is a major part of Jiff. Jiff’s focus is primarily on interoperability via the following: RFC 3339 specifies a format for fixed offset instants in time, in terms of a human readable civil datetime. For example, 2026-11-12T15:36:00-05:00 . This is the serialization format used by Timestamp . RFC 9557 extends and updates RFC 3339 to add time zone information. For example, 2026-11-12T15:36:00-05:00[America/New_York] . This is the serialization format used by ZonedDateTime . ISO 8601 covers mostly everything else, including durations and civil datetimes. For example, P5Y3MT20H is an ISO 8601 duration and 2026-11-12T15:30:00 is an ISO 8601 civil datetime whose corresponding instant in time is unknown. What Jiff actually implements is the Temporal RFC 9557 / ISO 8601 grammar for flexible parsing of datetimes from strings. For most use cases, it suffices to think in terms of RFC 3339, RFC 9557 or ISO 8601. But Jiff does support parsing strings that aren’t valid in any of those three specifications. For example, 2026-11-12[America/New_York] parses as if it was 2026-11-12T00:00:00[America/New_York] . In this section, we’ll take a tour of how Jiff does datetime formatting and printing. FromStr and Display Every datetime and duration type in Jiff implements the standard library FromStr and Display traits. This means that it’s natural to parse datetimes: let ts : Timestamp = "2026-10-31T05:15:00Z" . parse () ? ; and print them: println! ( " {ts} " ); Parsing is flexible, so even if there are components missing, parsing still succeeds. For example, without minutes or seconds, those components default to zero: let dt : civil :: DateTime = "2026-10-31T05" . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( dt . to_string (), "2026-10-31T05:00:00" ); Another example of flexible parsing is that if a string contains another date type, then one can parse that. For example, one can parse a date out of an ISO 8601 datetime: let d : civil :: Date = "2026-10-31T05:30" . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( d . to_string (), "2026-10-31" ); A ZonedDateTime always uses RFC 9557 syntax, which includes the IANA time zone identifier: let zdt : ZonedDateTime = "2026-10-31T05:30[Australia/Sydney]" . parse () ? ; // While the string we parsed didn't have any offset, // one was automatically added by consulting the time // zone definition for the civil datetime provided. assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-10-31T05:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); If you want to print a zoned datetime using only RFC 3339 syntax, then you can do so by formatting the timestamp directly with the zoned datetime’s offset: let zdt : ZonedDateTime = "2026-10-31T05:30[Australia/Sydney]" . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . timestamp (). display_with_offset ( zdt . offset ()). to_string (), "2026-10-31T05:30:00+11:00" , ); The Span and SignedDuration types also support the FromStr and Display traits via the ISO 8601 duration format. For example: use jiff :: { SignedDuration , Span }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let duration = "PT5H30M" ; let span : Span = duration . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( span . to_string (), "PT5H30M" ); let sdur : SignedDuration = duration . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( sdur . to_string (), "PT5H30M" ); Ok (()) } Since a Span is a hybrid duration that also supports calendar units, it can parse durations with calendar units and physical time units. A SignedDuration can only parse durations with physical time units: use jiff :: { SignedDuration , Span }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let duration = "P11Y2M28DT5H30M" ; let span : Span = duration . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( span . to_string (), "P11Y2M28DT5H30M" ); let err = duration . parse :: < SignedDuration > (). unwrap_err (); assert_eq! ( err . to_string (), "parsing ISO 8601 duration in this context requires \ that the duration contain a time component \ and no components of days or greater" , ); Ok (()) } The ISO 8601 duration format does, however, have some shortcomings that we’ll discuss in the next section. The “friendly” Duration Format Because ISO 8601 duration strings enjoy broad support, it is the default in Jiff for both Span and SignedDuration . However, it has two important shortcomings: It is difficult to read. For example, in P11Y2M28DT5H30M , the lack of whitespace makes the unit values and the unit labels all run together. An ISO 8601 duration cannot unambiguously represent all possible Span values. The second shortcoming is best seen with an example. Consider a Span that is 2000 milliseconds. If you convert this to an ISO 8601 duration string and then parse it back, you end up with 2 seconds instead: use jiff :: { Span , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let original = 2000. milliseconds (); assert_eq! ( original . to_string (), "PT2S" ); let got : Span = "PT2S" . parse () ? ; // The spans have different unit values! assert_eq! ( original . get_seconds (), 0 ); assert_eq! ( original . get_milliseconds (), 2000 ); assert_eq! ( got . get_seconds (), 2 ); assert_eq! ( got . get_milliseconds (), 0 ); Ok (()) } This might not be desirable for cases where you want a span’s string format to faithfully represent all possible distinct values of a span. For these two reasons, Jiff comes with its own bespoke “friendly” duration format. The friendly format is non-lossy and is meant to be easier to read for English speakers than the ISO 8601 duration format. Here are some examples that are all valid friendly durations: 40d 40 days 1y1d 1yr 1d 3d4h59m 3 days, 4 hours, 59 minutes 3d 4h 59m 2h30m 2h 30m 1mo 1w 1 week 1w4d 1 wk 4 days 1m 0.0021s 0s 0d 0 days 3 mins 34s 123ms 3 mins 34.123 secs 3 mins 34,123s 1y1mo1d1h1m1.1s 1yr 1mo 1day 1hr 1min 1.1sec 1 year, 1 month, 1 day, 1 hour, 1 minute 1.1 seconds 1 year, 1 month, 1 day, 01:01:01.1 Parsing a friendly duration is as easy as parsing an ISO 8601 duration: the FromStr implementations on both Span and SignedDuration support ISO 8601 durations and friendly durations simultaneously: let span : Span = "6y 10mo 3d 23h" . parse () ? ; // Recall that `Span::fieldwise` permits // equality comparisons on `Span` in a // unit-by-unit fashion. assert_eq! ( span . fieldwise (), 6. years (). months ( 10 ). days ( 3 ). hours ( 23 )); Printing a friendly duration does require a bit more effort, since it isn’t the default. Instead of Span::to_string() , one can use the “alternative” syntax via Rust’s formatting machinery: let span = 2000. milliseconds (); // This also demonstrates that our unit // values are preserved. assert_eq! ( format! ( " {span:#} " ), "2000ms" ); One can also use a lower level friendly printer to customize its output. For example, here’s how to write a span in the friendly format to an existing String using more spacing, longer unit labels and commas separating each unit: use jiff :: { fmt :: friendly , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { static PRINTER : friendly :: SpanPrinter = friendly :: SpanPrinter :: new () . comma_after_designator ( true ) . spacing ( friendly :: Spacing :: BetweenUnitsAndDesignators ) . designator ( friendly :: Designator :: Verbose ); let span = 6. years (). months ( 10 ). days ( 3 ). hours ( 23 ); let mut buf = String :: new (); PRINTER . print_span ( & span , & mut buf ) ? ; assert_eq! ( buf , "6 years, 10 months, 3 days, 23 hours" ); Ok (()) } See the jiff::fmt::friendly module for a lot more detail, including a grammar that precisely specifies the format supported. strptime and strftime The POSIX strptime and POSIX strftime routines are far from the ideal way to format and parse datetimes, but they are ubiquitous and most programmers are familiar with them. Because of their ubiquity, and because of the utility of being able to format and parse bespoke datetime formats, Jiff provides implementations of these routines that are mostly POSIX compatible. Every datetime type in Jiff comes with strptime and strftime routines. For example, to parse a civil date in the US month/day/year format: let date = civil :: Date :: strptime ( "%m/%d/%Y" , "11/13/2026" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( date . to_string (), "2026-11-13" ); Or to format a zoned datetime in a convenient to read representation for English speakers: let zdt = civil :: date ( 2026 , 11 , 13 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "Australia/Sydney" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . strftime ( "%a, %b %d, %Y %H:%M %Z" ). to_string (), "Fri, Nov 13, 2026 17:30 AEDT" , ); Callers can also use lower level APIs from jiff::fmt::strtime to get access to each parsed component individually: use jiff :: { civil , fmt :: strtime :: BrokenDownTime }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let tm = BrokenDownTime :: parse ( "%a, %b %d, %Y %H:%M" , "Fri, Nov 13, 2026 17:30" , ) ? ; assert_eq! ( tm . weekday (), Some ( civil :: Weekday :: Friday )); assert_eq! ( tm . month (), Some ( 11 )); assert_eq! ( tm . day (), Some ( 13 )); assert_eq! ( tm . year (), Some ( 2026 )); assert_eq! ( tm . hour (), Some ( 17 )); assert_eq! ( tm . minute (), Some ( 30 )); assert_eq! ( tm . second (), None ); Ok (()) } The jiff::fmt module While the above tour should cover most use cases, there are sometimes reasons for exerting more control over parsing or formatting. Or for supporting alternate formats like RFC 2822. The jiff::fmt module is meant to cover these use cases at the cost of more complex APIs. For example, consider parsing an RFC 2822 datetime string from a &[u8] (which lets callers avoid a UTF-8 validation check): use jiff :: fmt :: rfc2822 ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { static PARSER : rfc2822 :: DateTimeParser = rfc2822 :: DateTimeParser :: new (); let data = b "Sat, 13 Jul 2024 15:09:59 -0400" ; let ts = PARSER . parse_timestamp ( data ) ? ; assert_eq! ( ts . to_string (), "2024-07-13T19:09:59Z" ); Ok (()) } Another example shows how to change the default disambiguation strategy when the provided civil datetime is ambiguous. For example, Sydney, Australia moved the clocks backwards at 2026-04-05T03:00:00 local time. That is, they went from UTC offset +11 to UTC offset +10 . So what happens if we try to parse a time on the clock that is repeated as a result? use jiff :: ZonedDateTime ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt : ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney]" . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); Ok (()) } Here, the first occurrence of 02:30 is selected, just before Sydney leaves daylight saving time. Now, the data itself can actually select the desired offset: use jiff :: ZonedDateTime ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt : ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30+11:00[Australia/Sydney]" . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); let zdt : ZonedDateTime = "2026-04-05T02:30+10:00[Australia/Sydney]" . parse () ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+10:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); Ok (()) } But this happens because there is no ambiguity in the data. Since the offset is supplied, the exact instant in time is known. Going back to 2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney] , which is ambiguous because it could refer to two different instants in time, how do we modify the strategy for resolving that ambiguity? We can’t using the standard library FromStr trait, so we instead have to construct our own parser manually, just like we did for RFC 2822 parsing above. This example shows how to do that and all of the different disambiguation options. Remember, UTC offset +11:00 corresponds to the first occurrence of 2026-04-05T02:30 on the clocks of folks in Sydney while UTC offset +10:00 corresponds to the second occurrence. use jiff :: { fmt :: temporal :: DateTimeParser , tz :: Disambiguation }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let string = "2026-04-05T02:30[Australia/Sydney]" ; // "compatible" is the default strategy, which selects // the earlier time in a fold (usually moving from daylight // saving time to standard time) and the later time in a // gap (usually moving from standard time to daylight // saving time). let parser = DateTimeParser :: new (). disambiguation ( Disambiguation :: Compatible ); let zdt = parser . parse_zoned_datetime ( string ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); // "earlier" always selects the first occurrence // in a fold, or the time before a gap. // So this is the same as compatible in this case, // since our civil time is in a fold. let parser = DateTimeParser :: new (). disambiguation ( Disambiguation :: Earlier ); let zdt = parser . parse_zoned_datetime ( string ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+11:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); // "later" always selects the second occurrence // in a fold, or the time after a gap. // So this is different from "compatible" for a // fold. Notice that the UTC +10:00 offset is // chosen. let parser = DateTimeParser :: new (). disambiguation ( Disambiguation :: Later ); let zdt = parser . parse_zoned_datetime ( string ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2026-04-05T02:30:00+10:00[Australia/Sydney]" ); // "reject" means that if the instant is ambiguous, // then an error is returned. let parser = DateTimeParser :: new (). disambiguation ( Disambiguation :: Reject ); let err = parser . parse_zoned_datetime ( string ). unwrap_err (); assert_eq! ( err . to_string (), "error converting datetime to instant \ in time zone Australia/Sydney: \ datetime is ambiguous since it falls \ into a fold between offsets +11 and +10" , ); Ok (()) } The jiff::fmt module contains lots of other goodies that we won’t cover here, including, but not limited to: The ability to format directly into an existing allocation. Parsing a datetime into its individual components. Helpers for serde integration. Locale Sensitive Formatting via ICU4X Integration No section on datetime formatting would be complete without addressing locales. In this context, a locale is a set of user preferences used for formatting datetimes. This is useful when you want to present a datetime to an end user that doesn’t expect standard formats from RFC 3339 , RFC 9557 or ISO 8601 . Jiff itself does not provide any facilities for dealing with locales. Instead, users can opt into this support via the ICU4X project. To make conversions between Jiff and ICU4X, the jiff-icu integration crate can be used. Here’s an example showing how to format a zoned datetime in the fr-LA locale: (You’ll need to run cargo add icu jiff-icu to your project for this to work.) use icu :: { calendar :: Iso , datetime :: { fieldsets , DateTimeFormatter }, locale :: locale , time :: { zone :: models :: AtTime , TimeZoneInfo }, }; use jiff :: ZonedDateTime ; use jiff_icu :: ConvertFrom as _ ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { // Firstly, do a conversion from Jiff's zoned datetime to ICU's. let jiff_zdt : ZonedDateTime = "2024-09-10T23:37:20-04[America/New_York]" . parse () ? ; let icu_zdt = icu :: time :: ZonedDateTime :: < Iso , TimeZoneInfo < AtTime >> :: convert_from ( & jiff_zdt , ); // Second, create a datetime formatter for the fr-LA locale: let formatter = DateTimeFormatter :: try_new ( locale! ( "fr-LA" ). into (), fieldsets :: YMDET :: medium (). with_zone ( fieldsets :: zone :: SpecificLong ), ) ? ; // Thirdly, format the zoned datetime. assert_eq! ( formatter . format ( & icu_zdt ). to_string (), "mar. 10 sept. 2024, 23:37:20 heure d’été de l’Est nord-américain" , ); Ok (()) } The ICU4X API has a lot of options for customizing datetime formatting. Exploring it further is outside the scope of this blog. Date Manipulation Jiff provides many methods on its datetime types to make using them as comfortable and error-free as possible. Date Basics Every datetime type provides a new constructor that lets callers build it from its constituent parts. In most cases, this constructor is fallible. For example: use jiff :: civil :: Date ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d = Date :: new ( 2024 , 2 , 29 ) ? ; // All datetime types have convenient // accessors for each of their components. assert_eq! ( d . year (), 2024 ); assert_eq! ( d . month (), 2 ); assert_eq! ( d . day (), 29 ); let err = Date :: new ( 2025 , 2 , 29 ). unwrap_err (); assert_eq! ( err . to_string (), "parameter 'day' for `2025-02` is invalid, must be in range `1..=28`" , ); Ok (()) } Because creating dates is so common, there is a shorthand for doing so when you know the inputs are valid: let d = const { civil :: date ( 2024 , 2 , 29 ) }; assert_eq! ( d . year (), 2024 ); assert_eq! ( d . month (), 2 ); assert_eq! ( d . day (), 29 ); That is, civil::date is a const function that will panic if its inputs are invalid. It should only be used with inputs that are known to be valid. It would, for example, be inappropriate to use this with user provided values. Because of the const block above, if you try to provide invalid values, you’ll get a compiler error. For datetime types that represent an instant in time (i.e., ZonedDateTime and Timestamp ), there is also a now() constructor for getting the current time: use jiff :: { Timestamp , ZonedDateTime }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let now = Timestamp :: now (); println! ( " {now} " ); // Example output: 2026-11-15T14:17:21.80099287Z // This will automatically fetch your system's configured time zone. let now = ZonedDateTime :: now (); println! ( " {now} " ); // Example output: 2026-11-15T09:17:21.80102125-05:00[America/New_York] Ok (()) } In addition to constructors, new date values can be constructed from old date values using the Date::with API: let d1 = const { civil :: date ( 2024 , 2 , 29 ) }; // This API doesn't break just because 31 // is supplied before a month that has 31 // days. Any order is fine! This is because // errors are deferred until `build()` is // called. let d2 = d1 . with (). day ( 31 ). month ( 3 ). build () ? ; assert_eq! ( d2 . to_string (), "2024-03-31" ); Once you have a date, there are oodles of APIs available: let d = civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 10 ); assert_eq! ( d . weekday (), civil :: Weekday :: Thursday ); assert_eq! ( d . first_of_year (), civil :: date ( 2025 , 1 , 1 )); assert_eq! ( d . last_of_year (), civil :: date ( 2025 , 12 , 31 )); assert_eq! ( d . first_of_month (), civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 1 )); assert_eq! ( d . last_of_month (), civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 31 )); assert_eq! ( d . yesterday () ? , civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 9 )); assert_eq! ( d . tomorrow () ? , civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 11 )); Moreover, because of the datetime onion , all of these APIs are also available on civil::DateTime and ZonedDateTime : let create_zdt = | date : civil :: Date | -> Result < ZonedDateTime , jiff :: Error > { date . at ( 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) }; let zdt = create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 10 )) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . weekday (), civil :: Weekday :: Thursday ); assert_eq! ( zdt . first_of_year () ? , create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 1 , 1 )) ? ); assert_eq! ( zdt . last_of_year () ? , create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 12 , 31 )) ? ); assert_eq! ( zdt . first_of_month () ? , create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 1 )) ? ); assert_eq! ( zdt . last_of_month () ? , create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 31 )) ? ); assert_eq! ( zdt . yesterday () ? , create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 9 )) ? ); assert_eq! ( zdt . tomorrow () ? , create_zdt ( civil :: date ( 2025 , 7 , 11 )) ? ); These routines on ZonedDateTime also take time zone transitions into account. For example, ZonedDateTime knows that tomorrow() doesn’t always add 24 hours: // On 2024-11-03 at 2AM in New York, time was rolled // back 1 hour in the transition from daylight saving // time to standard time. That means 2024-11-03 was // actually 25 hours long in New York. let zdt = civil :: date ( 2024 , 11 , 2 ). at ( 17 , 25 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let tomorrow = zdt . tomorrow () ? ; assert_eq! ( tomorrow . datetime (), civil :: date ( 2024 , 11 , 3 ). at ( 17 , 25 , 0 , 0 )); // The physical time difference between them is 25 hours! let span = tomorrow - zdt ; assert_eq! ( format! ( " {span:#} " ), "25h" ); NOTE : We’ll talk about date arithmetic in the next section. When ZonedDateTime::tomorrow() (among other APIs that produce a ZonedDateTime ) would land in a gap or a fold, the “compatible” disambiguation strategy is chosen automatically: // For a zoned datetime that lands // in a fold, the earlier instant is // chosen by default. let zdt = civil :: date ( 2024 , 11 , 2 ). at ( 1 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let tomorrow = zdt . tomorrow () ? ; assert_eq! ( tomorrow . to_string (), "2024-11-03T01:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]" ); // And for a gap, the later instant // is chosen by default. let zdt = civil :: date ( 2024 , 3 , 9 ). at ( 2 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let tomorrow = zdt . tomorrow () ? ; assert_eq! ( tomorrow . to_string (), "2024-03-10T03:30:00-04:00[America/New_York]" ); To override this behavior, you can drop down to civil datetimes, perform the operation, and then use TimeZone::to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime to control the exact disambiguation strategy: // For a zoned datetime that lands // in a fold, the earlier instant is // chosen by default. But let's say // we want the later instant. let zdt = civil :: date ( 2024 , 11 , 2 ). at ( 1 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let tomorrow = zdt . time_zone () . to_ambiguous_zoned_datetime ( zdt . datetime (). tomorrow () ? ) . later () ? ; assert_eq! ( tomorrow . to_string (), // Notice that the offset is now -05, // which corresponds to the later // instant. "2024-11-03T01:30:00-05:00[America/New_York]" ); There are a few other methods of note on date types that are worth mentioning. First is the ability to query for things like, “The Thursday after next” or “The last Sunday of the month.” The former can be answered by the nth_weekday API: let zdt1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 10 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt1 . weekday (), civil :: Weekday :: Wednesday ); // Not this Thursday, but the next! let zdt2 = zdt1 . nth_weekday ( 2 , civil :: Weekday :: Thursday ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt2 . weekday (), civil :: Weekday :: Thursday ); assert_eq! ( zdt2 . date (), civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 18 )); While the latter can be answered by the nth_weekday_of_month API: let zdt1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 10 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt1 . weekday (), civil :: Weekday :: Wednesday ); // The last Sunday of this month. let zdt2 = zdt1 . nth_weekday_of_month ( - 1 , civil :: Weekday :: Sunday ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt2 . weekday (), civil :: Weekday :: Sunday ); assert_eq! ( zdt2 . date (), civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 28 )); Finally, users can access a convenient time series iterator via series : use jiff :: { civil , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let start = civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 10 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let mut dates = vec! []; // Every week for 8 weeks. for zdt in start . series ( 1. week ()). take ( 8 ) { dates . push ( zdt ); } assert_eq! ( dates , vec! [ civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 10 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 17 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 24 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 31 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 8 , 7 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 8 , 14 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 8 , 21 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 8 , 28 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? , ] ); Ok (()) } All of these methods are also available on civil::Date and civil::DateTime , which should make it very natural to move between them. Date Arithmetic All datetime types in Jiff support adding and subtracting durations, and finding the span of time between two datetime values. Let’s start with a civil::Date : use jiff :: { civil , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 30 ); let d2 = d1 + 2. days (); assert_eq! ( d2 , civil :: date ( 2024 , 8 , 1 )); Ok (()) } Here we make use of the std::ops::Add trait implementation for civil::Date . The downside of using this, though, is that if the date value goes out of range, then it panics. That may or may not be acceptable. But if you’re dealing with user inputs, then you should use Date::checked_add instead: use jiff :: { civil , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 30 ); let d2 = d1 . checked_add ( 2. days ()) ? ; assert_eq! ( d2 , civil :: date ( 2024 , 8 , 1 )); Ok (()) } Let’s take a look at a few other examples involving months and years: let d = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ); assert_eq! ( d . checked_add ( 1. month ()) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 6 , 30 )); assert_eq! ( d . checked_add ( 2. months ()) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 7 , 31 )); let d = civil :: date ( 2025 , 1 , 31 ); assert_eq! ( d . checked_add ( 1. month ()) ? , civil :: date ( 2025 , 2 , 28 )); let d = civil :: date ( 2024 , 2 , 29 ); let span = 1. year (). months ( 2 ). days ( 5 ); assert_eq! ( d . checked_add ( span ) ? , civil :: date ( 2025 , 5 , 4 )); As with other methods on Date , they are also available on ZonedDateTime : let d = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ). at ( 13 , 45 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( d . checked_add ( 1. month ()) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 6 , 30 ). at ( 13 , 45 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ); If we take a look at the type signature for ZonedDateTime::checked_add , we can see that it’s actually polymorphic: pub fn checked_add < A : Into < ZonedDateTimeArithmetic >> ( & self , duration : A , ) -> Result < ZonedDateTime , Error > Specifically, it accepts anything that can be converted into a ZonedDateTimeArithmetic . In this case, there are From trait implementations for the following types: Span SignedDuration std::time::Duration This means that ZonedDateTime::checked_add can accept any one of these duration values: use jiff :: { civil , SignedDuration }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ). at ( 13 , 45 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( d . checked_add ( SignedDuration :: from_mins ( 45 )) ? , civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ). at ( 14 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ); Ok (()) } This type of polymorphism is common in Jiff. Here, it is merely used to provide a convenient way to use multiple duration types. But as we’ll see, it’s also used to provide an extension point for configuration options that control how the operation works. In addition to adding or subtracting durations from datetime values, one can also compute the duration between two datetime values. For example, to get the number of days between two dates: use jiff :: { civil , ToSpan }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let d1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ); let d2 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 9 , 30 ); assert_eq! ( d2 - d1 , 122. days (). fieldwise ()); Ok (()) } Similarly, we can use Date::until to compute the span between dates: let d1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ); let d2 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 9 , 30 ); assert_eq! ( d1 . until ( d2 ) ? , 122. days (). fieldwise ()); Like with Date::checked_add , this routine is also available at ZonedDateTime::until : let zdt1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let zdt2 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 9 , 30 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt1 . until ( & zdt2 ) ? , 2928. hours (). fieldwise ()); Notice though that hours, instead of days, are returned. This is because two ZonedDateTime values might be in different time zones. Since a ZonedDateTime is fundamentally an instant in time, and because days might be of varying length depending on the time zone, defaulting to hours as the largest possible unit means subtracting two zoned datetimes will always succeed. However, we can request larger units in the duration returned by passing additional options. Notably, ZonedDateTime::until is polymorphic: pub fn until < 'a , A : Into < ZonedDateTimeDifference < 'a >>> ( & self , other : A , ) -> Result < Span , Error > That is, callers aren’t just limited to passing a ZonedDateTime here, but anything that can be converted to a ZonedDateTimeDifference . Here is one such example, where we can override the largest units returned in the duration: use jiff :: { civil , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt1 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let zdt2 = civil :: date ( 2024 , 9 , 30 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt1 . until (( Unit :: Month , & zdt2 )) ? , 3. months (). days ( 30 ). fieldwise () ); Ok (()) } A ZonedDateTimeDifference provides much more powerful configuration options for rounding the span returned. Take this example, which produces a span with many unit values: use jiff :: { civil :: date , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt1 = date ( 2024 , 5 , 15 ). at ( 14 , 30 , 54 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let zdt2 = date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ) . at ( 19 , 13 , 27 , 123_456_789 ) . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt1 . until (( Unit :: Day , & zdt2 )) ? , 16. days () . hours ( 4 ) . minutes ( 42 ) . seconds ( 33 ) . milliseconds ( 123 ) . microseconds ( 456 ) . nanoseconds ( 789 ) . fieldwise (), ); Ok (()) } This might be too much precision to show to an end user. Instead, perhaps we’d like to round the span to the nearest half-hour. We can do this by building a ZonedDateTimeDifference explicitly and configuring its options: use jiff :: { civil :: date , RoundMode , ToSpan , Unit , ZonedDateTimeDifference }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt1 = date ( 2024 , 5 , 15 ). at ( 14 , 30 , 54 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let zdt2 = date ( 2024 , 5 , 31 ) . at ( 19 , 13 , 27 , 123_456_789 ) . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let difference = ZonedDateTimeDifference :: new ( & zdt2 ) . largest ( Unit :: Day ) . smallest ( Unit :: Minute ) . increment ( 30 ) . mode ( RoundMode :: HalfExpand ); assert_eq! ( zdt1 . until ( difference ) ? , 16. days (). hours ( 4 ). minutes ( 30 ). fieldwise (), ); Ok (()) } Note also that rounding a span takes time zone transitions like daylight saving time into account. For example, let’s take 2024-11-02 17:30 and 2024-11-03 04:45 in New York. Because New York stopped daylight saving time at 2AM on 2024-11-03, the amount of physical time between them is 12 hours and 15 minutes: let zdt1 = date ( 2024 , 11 , 2 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let zdt2 = date ( 2024 , 11 , 3 ). at ( 4 , 45 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt2 - zdt1 , 12. hours (). minutes ( 15 ). fieldwise ()); Normally, if we rounded to the nearest day, this would round up to 1 day. But since the midpoint of this particular day is actually 12 hours and 30 minutes, this duration will round down to 0 days when we request it: use jiff :: { civil :: date , RoundMode , ToSpan , Unit , ZonedDateTimeDifference }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt1 = date ( 2024 , 11 , 2 ). at ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let zdt2 = date ( 2024 , 11 , 3 ). at ( 4 , 45 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; let difference = ZonedDateTimeDifference :: new ( & zdt2 ) . largest ( Unit :: Day ) . smallest ( Unit :: Day ) . mode ( RoundMode :: HalfExpand ); assert_eq! ( zdt1 . until ( difference ) ? , 0. days (). fieldwise ()); Ok (()) } Next we’ll continue our discussion of rounding, but when applied to datetimes themselves. Date Rounding Date rounding in Jiff is limited to units of days or lower. Therefore, it’s only available on ZonedDateTime , Timestamp , civil::DateTime , civil::Time but not civil::Date . A common example for rounding a datetime is to reduce precision. For example, a system clock might provide nanosecond precision, but maybe we only care about the nearest half-hour: use jiff :: { civil :: date , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let zdt = date ( 2024 , 11 , 2 ) . at ( 17 , 46 , 20 , 123_456_789 ) . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2024-11-02T17:46:20.123456789-04:00[America/New_York]" ); // Round to the nearest half hour. let rounded = zdt . round (( Unit :: Minute , 30 )) ? ; assert_eq! ( rounded . to_string (), "2024-11-02T18:00:00-04:00[America/New_York]" ); Ok (()) } As with rounding spans, rounding a ZonedDateTime is aware of time zone transitions: let zdt = date ( 2024 , 11 , 3 ) . at ( 11 , 45 , 20 , 123_456_789 ) . in_tz ( "America/New_York" ) ? ; // Round to the nearest day. let rounded = zdt . round ( Unit :: Day ) ? ; assert_eq! ( rounded . to_string (), "2024-11-04T00:00:00-05:00[America/New_York]" ); Notice that in the above example, our time of 11:45AM is before noon, yet the result still rounds up to the next day. This is because the midpoint for this day is 11:30AM since, by 11:30AM, 12.5 hours have already elapsed because of the repeated 1AM hour in the move away from daylight saving time in New York. Other Calendars Jiff itself doesn’t support any calendars other than the proleptic Gregorian calendar. One can instead use the ICU4X crate to work in non-Gregorian calendars, and convert between datetime types using the jiff-icu crate: (Use cargo add icu jiff-icu to make this example work.) use icu :: { calendar :: { types :: Month , Date as IcuDate }, time :: { DateTime as IcuDateTime , Time as IcuTime }, }; use jiff :: civil :: DateTime ; use jiff_icu :: ConvertTryFrom as _ ; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { // Firstly, create an ICU datetime using the Hebrew calendar. let datetime = IcuDateTime { date : IcuDate :: try_new_hebrew_v2 ( 5785 , Month :: new ( 5 ), 4 ) ? , time : IcuTime :: try_new ( 17 , 30 , 0 , 0 ) ? , }; // Secondly, convert it to a civil datetime. // This will automatically use ICU to convert // the date from the Hebrew calendar to the // Gregorian (or ISO) calendar. let zdt = DateTime :: convert_try_from ( datetime ) ? ; assert_eq! ( zdt . to_string (), "2025-02-02T17:30:00" ); Ok (()) } The ICU4X API supports many more calendars . Which DateTime Type Do I Use? There are 3 potentially confusable datetime types in Jiff: civil::DateTime Timestamp ZonedDateTime When should you use each one versus the other? To a first approximation, if you can use a ZonedDateTime , then that is probably the type you want to reach for. It represents a specific instant in time in a particular geographic location. That is, it has both a Timestamp and a TimeZone . If you only ever need to work in UTC or just deal with system time, then a Timestamp is probably the right choice. This is useful for representing a specific instant in time that is not connected to any time zone. A civil::DateTime is useful in contexts where you don’t care about a specific instant in time and when calcuations should be done independent of time zone. For example, when parsing datetime information from a user interface datetime picker. Remember that both a civil::DateTime and a Timestamp can be converted to a ZonedDateTime by supplying a time zone. Span Manipulation We’ve already seen how to add spans to datetime values and how to get spans as a difference between datetime values. But we haven’t yet explored the APIs available on a Span itself. First and foremost, we can build a Span through its constructor, which returns a Span with all of its units set to 0 : use jiff :: Span ; let span = Span :: new (); A Span is both Copy and immutable. We can create new spans through method chaining: let span = Span :: new (). hours ( 1 ). minutes ( 30 ); assert_eq! ( span . to_string (), "PT1H30M" ); Or we can use the ToSpan convenience trait, which adds methods on integer types for constructing spans: use jiff :: ToSpan ; let span = 1. hour (). minutes ( 30 ); assert_eq! ( span . to_string (), "PT1H30M" ); Note though that methods like Span::hours and ToSpan::hours will panic when the integer is outside the limits of what Span supports. This is fine when your spans are literals in your program, since a panic would indicate a bug. But if your inputs come from an end user, it’s better to use fallible methods: let span = Span :: new (). try_hours ( 1 ) ? . try_minutes ( 30 ) ? ; assert_eq! ( span . to_string (), "PT1H30M" ); Spans preserve each individual unit value. This means that 90 minutes and 1 hour 30 minutes, while they represent the same duration, are actually different values in memory: let span1 = 1. hour (). minutes ( 30 ); let span2 = 90. minutes (); assert_eq! ( span1 . to_string (), "PT1H30M" ); assert_eq! ( span2 . to_string (), "PT90M" ); This permits callers maximum flexibility when it comes to representing durations. This makes it possible to represent durations in a specific unit even when they add up to larger units. For example, the runtime duration of films is typically conveyed in minutes, even when the runtime exceeds one hour. This can be adjusted programmatically using Span::round : use jiff :: { SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span1 = 1. hour (). minutes ( 30 ); let span2 = span1 . round ( SpanRound :: new (). largest ( Unit :: Minute )) ? ; assert_eq! ( span2 . to_string (), "PT90M" ); Ok (()) } You can go the other way as well: use jiff :: { SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span1 = 90. minutes (); let span2 = span1 . round ( SpanRound :: new (). largest ( Unit :: Hour )) ? ; assert_eq! ( span2 . to_string (), "PT1H30M" ); Ok (()) } Neither of these examples do actual rounding, despite the name of the API. Instead, since we’re only setting the largest unit, this API is doing unit balancing. Unit balancing is when all unit values rollover into larger units up until the largest configured unit. This works even for calendar units too, but you need to provide a relative date: use jiff :: { civil , SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 2756. hours (); let dt = civil :: date ( 2020 , 1 , 1 ). at ( 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 ); let round = SpanRound :: new (). largest ( Unit :: Year ). relative ( dt ); assert_eq! ( span . round ( round ) ? . to_friendly (), "3mo 23d 20h" ); Ok (()) } Without a relative date, it’s not possible to know how many hours are in a single month. That is, once calendar units are involved, a span cannot be interpreted as a physical duration of time until some context is applied. The same even applies to days themselves, since days can sometimes be more or less than 24 hours. Take the above example. What happens if we use a zoned datetime as our relative date instead? use jiff :: { civil , SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 2756. hours (); let zdt = civil :: date ( 2020 , 1 , 1 ). at ( 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 ). in_tz ( "Europe/Rome" ) ? ; let round = SpanRound :: new (). largest ( Unit :: Year ). relative ( & zdt ); assert_eq! ( span . round ( round ) ? . to_friendly (), "3mo 23d 21h" ); Ok (()) } Notice that the duration’s hour component changed from 20 to 21 . Why? Because we started with 2756 hour in both cases and because 2020-03-29 in Rome was only 23 hours long (in a move from standard time to daylight saving time). That means that one of those days in 3mo 23d was only 23 hours long. So an extra hour needed to be added to make up for it. The round API can also do actual rounding: use jiff :: { SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 2. hours (). minutes ( 30 ); let round = SpanRound :: new (). smallest ( Unit :: Hour ); assert_eq! ( span . round ( round ) ? . to_friendly (), "3h" ); Ok (()) } You can also change its rounding mode from the default (“half-expand”, or like you were taught rounding in school) to truncation (or one of several other modes): use jiff :: { RoundMode , SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 2. hours (). minutes ( 30 ); let round = SpanRound :: new (). smallest ( Unit :: Hour ). mode ( RoundMode :: Trunc ); assert_eq! ( span . round ( round ) ? . to_friendly (), "2h" ); Ok (()) } One can also specify a rounding increment to round to the nearest unit value. For example, to the nearest half-hour: use jiff :: { SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 2. hours (). minutes ( 31 ); let round = SpanRound :: new (). smallest ( Unit :: Minute ). increment ( 30 ); assert_eq! ( span . round ( round ) ? . to_friendly (), "2h 30m" ); Ok (()) } Because a Span value cannot easily be compared correctly based purely on its value in memory, a dedicated comparison Span::compare routine is provided: let span1 = 2. hours (); let span2 = 120. minutes (); assert! ( span1 . compare ( span2 ) ? . is_eq ()); Also, one can convert a Span to a floating point value in terms of any unit. For example: use jiff :: { ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 90. minutes (); assert_eq! ( span . total ( Unit :: Hour ) ? , 1.5 ); Ok (()) } Converting to calendar units requires a relative date for the same reasons discussed above: use jiff :: { civil , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 24. hours (); assert_eq! ( span . total (( Unit :: Month , civil :: date ( 2026 , 6 , 1 ))) ? , 0.03333333333333333 ); assert_eq! ( span . total (( Unit :: Month , civil :: date ( 2026 , 7 , 1 ))) ? , 0.03225806451612903 ); Ok (()) } Conclusion So far, we’ve explored a good chunk of Jiff’s API. We didn’t talk about every nook and cranny, but I think we’ve covered the most important pieces. We’ll wrap up by briefly discussing motivation and inspiration. Motivation Whenever I needed datetime handling in Rust, I always got confused. Should I use chrono or time ? How do I get my local time from a timestamp? How do I use my system’s time zone database? How do I do calendar arithmetic? Before I started working on Jiff, this confusion got annoying enough for me to consider writing my own crate. I felt like the APIs of both chrono and time could be improved upon. I personally found the domain quite interesting and so set out to build something better. Why not improve on an existing solution, like chrono or time , instead of adding yet another choice into the ecosystem? I do think there are material downsides of having too many choices, but I had concluded that both chrono and time (in 2024) had reached a local maximum. Moreover, in 2024, I was not an expert in datetime handling. It took building a datetime library to become one. So convincing crate maintainers to go in a radically different direction would have been a tall order. Jiff’s design and comparison documentation contain much more detail regarding the motivation and specific examples between Jiff, chrono and time . Inspiration Jiff is heavily inspired by Temporal , which is JavaScript’s standard library solution for date and time management. Jiff inherits API design, functionality and even parsing/formatting of datetime values. Note though that Jiff is not and does not aim to be a 100% compatible implementation of the Temporal specification. Jiff is meant to be a Rust ecosystem library first and foremost. With that said, if you’re familiar with Temporal and Rust, then it’s likely you’ll find Jiff to be a relatively straightforward translation of Temporal’s API to Rust. This example shows how to use Temporal to round a calendar span to the nearest number of days relative to a date: const duration = Temporal . Duration . from ({ months : 1 , days : 1 , hours : 1 }); const roundedDuration = duration . round ({ largestUnit : "days" , smallestUnit : "days" , relativeTo : Temporal . PlainDateTime . from ( "2022-01-01" ), }); console . log ( roundedDuration ); // "P32D" And here’s the equivalent operation in Jiff: use jiff :: { SpanRound , ToSpan , Unit }; fn main () -> anyhow :: Result < () > { let span = 1. month (). days ( 1 ). hours ( 1 ); let rounded_span = span . round ( SpanRound :: new () . largest ( Unit :: Day ) . smallest ( Unit :: Day ) . relative ( "2022-01-01" . parse :: < jiff :: civil :: Date > () ? ), ) ? ; assert_eq! ( rounded_span . to_string (), "P32D" ); Ok (()) } The main difference between these examples is that Jiff’s duration type is named Span instead of Duration . This was done to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Duration type. Here are some other differences: Temporal’s Instant type in Jiff is named Timestamp in order to avoid confusion with Rust’s standard library std::time::Instant type. Temporal’s “plain” date and time types are called “civil” in Jiff. Jiff only supports the Gregorian calendar. Jiff’s datetime range only extends to +/- 9999, whereas Temporal’s range is larger. It’s easy to say that without Temporal, Jiff wouldn’t exist in its current form today. All content is dual licensed under the UNLICENSE and MIT licenses. Powered by Hugo & Pixyll

title: Grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays
body_text: Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains | Cornell Chronicle Skip to main content Toggle navigation Search Cornell University Cornell.edu Media Relations Search Cornell University Cornell Chronicle Topics Architecture & Design Artificial Intelligence Arts & Humanities Business, Economics & Entrepreneurship Computing & Information Sciences Energy, Environment & Sustainability Food & Agriculture Global Reach Health, Nutrition & Medicine Law, Government & Public Policy Life Sciences & Veterinary Medicine Physical Sciences & Engineering Social & Behavioral Sciences Research Matters Campus & Community News & Events Local Impact NYS Impact New York City Public Engagement Features Photos of the Week Student Life Staff News Big Red Sports Inclusion and Belonging University Statements In Memory Around Cornell All Stories Podcast Media Relations Cornellians Credit: Sreang Hok/Cornell University A solar farm in Lansing, New York. Sheep grazing in solar fields offers farmers economic, ecological gains By Krisy Gashler College of Agriculture and Life Sciences October 14, 2026 Two new research papers shed light on the growing practice of grazing sheep in fields with solar arrays. One demonstrates that, in the right numbers, sheep grazing increases populations of beneficial insects like bees and lady beetles compared to mowing around solar panels. The other research describes a decision-making support tool to help farmers profitably grow their solar grazing herds. A team from the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences (CALS) found that when two sheep per hectare graze around solar arrays, the abundance of wild bees, honey bees and lady beetles jumped by 38%, compared to a control plot that was mowed. The increase was driven primarily by an 83% increase in honey bees alone, according to the team’s findings in “ Low solar-grazing densities support beneficial insects in agrivoltaic systems ,” published Oct. 7 in Environmental Research Letters. “Sheep grazing and beneficial insect habitat are two prominent conversation topics around solar development right now,” said Leana Zoller, the paper’s first author and a postdoctoral associate in natural resources in the Cornell CALS Ashley School of Global Development and the Environment. “But what’s been missing is research that treats them as parts of the same system. When we talk about sustainable solar development, integrating these discussions into a single framework is really helpful to farmers and community decision makers.” For three years, Zoller and a team of entomologists, ecologists and animal and plant scientists tested various stocking rates – how many sheep per hectare are allowed to graze a certain plot of land – using Cornell’s teaching sheep grazing at the university-owned  Cascadilla Community Solar Farm in Dryden, New York. At four sheep per hectare, they found beneficial insect abundance was similar to the mowed control site, while vegetation management effectiveness was greater than at two sheep per hectare. At eight sheep per hectare, vegetation management was maximized and sheep flock health remained high, but honey bee abundance dropped by 45%. “We zeroed in on stocking rates because that’s a concrete number that sheep farmers understand and work with every day, and we want this research to be useful,” said  Steve Grodsky , paper senior author and assistant professor of natural resources in the Ashley School. “With solar grazing, people, energy, agricultural animals, plants and insects are all part of this ecosystem. We’re trying to understand the connections between those pieces so that when solar developers, municipalities looking at solar development, or farmers are faced with a decision, they can have scientific information about potential trade-offs and synergies.” Grodsky is also assistant unit leader of the U.S. Geological Survey New York Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit. Additional co-authors are sheep farmer and solar grazing consultant Nikola Kochendoerfer, Ph.D. ’20;  Antonio DiTommaso , professor in the School of Integrative Plant Science; John Losey , professor of entomology;  Scott McArt , Ph.D. ’12, associate professor of entomology; Paige Muñiz, formerly a technician in McArt’s lab; and  Todd Ugine , Ph.D. ’04, research associate in Losey’s lab, all in CALS.  Sarah Carson , director of Cornell’s Campus Sustainability Office, was key in coordinating site access between researchers and the solar company that manages the Cascadilla solar farm. Another Cornell research team, from the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, has developed a tool that helps farmers whose sheep graze in solar arrays to make better decisions about their operation. The team described the tool in “ Flock Management for Solar Grazing ,” which published Sept. 28 in Manufacturing & Service Operations Management. After a chance encounter with Caleb Scott, Ithaca-based sheep farmer and founder of  United Agrivoltaics ,  Vincent Slaugh , assistant professor at the Cornell Peter and Stephanie Nolan School of Hotel Administration and first author of the paper, began thinking through the economics and logistics of solar grazing. He recruited  Linwei Xin , associate professor of operations research and information engineering, and  Shane Henderson , Charles W. Lake, Jr. Professor in Productivity, both in the Cornell Duffield College of Engineering, to work on the topic. Together, they developed a spreadsheet-based model that helps sheep farmers to optimize procurement and sales decisions, based on factors like target flock size, costs, anticipated revenues, and expected vegetation in particular solar sites; if a farmer doesn’t have enough sheep to keep the grass down, they’ll have to cut it some other way. It also helps solar developers understand growers’ needs and develop contracts that are more profitable and sustainable for all parties long-term. United Agrivoltaics has already incorporated the tool into its onboarding process. Slaugh sees opportunity for U.S. shepherds to grow their operations – especially with solar contracts offering a steady source of income and animal feed. Current domestic sheep production for meat and wool doesn’t come close to meeting domestic demand; about  half of all lamb and mutton consumed in the U.S. is imported , primarily from New Zealand and Australia. “If we grow the sheep industry, will the American diet eventually include more lamb? Could that be a side effect of the solar energy revolution? I think the answer is very likely yes,” Slaugh said. “And then when that happens, we’d expect processors and supporting industries to come back, for banks to be willing to give more loans, and for supply chains to follow. All of that grows the economy, and rural economies in particular.” Kochendoerfer, who grazes 700 ewes on solar installations in New York and Vermont, said that economy is already growing.  “I work with a lot of farms that are now scaling up because of solar,” Kochendoerfer said. “There is a new wave of sheep farmers who are capitalizing on this access to good land. With solar grazing, you get paid to graze as opposed to having to pay to graze. That leads to sustainable, meaningful economic income that these farmers can use to expand, build a barn, buy equipment or hire someone. It’s enabling a lot of folks to build sound, viable agricultural businesses.” Funding for these research projects came from the Cornell Atkinson Center for Sustainability, the National Institute for Food and Agriculture and the National Science Foundation. Krisy Gashler is a writer for the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences. title: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch
body_text: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch | Cornell Chronicle Skip to main content Toggle navigation Search Cornell University Cornell.edu Media Relations Search Cornell University Cornell Chronicle Topics Architecture & Design Artificial Intelligence Arts & Humanities Business, Economics & Entrepreneurship Computing & Information Sciences Energy, Environment & Sustainability Food & Agriculture Global Reach Health, Nutrition & Medicine Law, Government & Public Policy Life Sciences & Veterinary Medicine Physical Sciences & Engineering Social & Behavioral Sciences Research Matters Campus & Community News & Events Local Impact NYS Impact New York City Public Engagement Features Photos of the Week Student Life Staff News Big Red Sports Inclusion and Belonging University Statements In Memory Around Cornell All Stories Podcast Media Relations Cornellians Pause Video Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch By Patricia Waldron Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science November 11, 2026 For the first time, researchers can track the movement of a person’s entire body with ultrasonic sound waves, using just an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model – all while ensuring privacy and efficiency. The new technology, called EchoMotion, was developed by Cornell’s  Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab , directed by Cheng Zhang , associate professor of information science in the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. It uses the built-in speaker and microphone on a commercial smartwatch to determine a person’s body position using a sonar-like sensing system. Once EchoMotion is integrated into commercial wearables or virtual reality (VR) systems, it could be used for tracking workouts, daily activities and progress on physical rehabilitation. EchoMotion represents a scalable approach that can use AI to understand human behaviors in the real world, Zheng said. He presented the paper, “ EchoMotion: Towards Full-Body Pose Tracking with a Single Smartwatch Using Active Acoustic Sensing ,” at the Association for Computing Machinery international joint conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing and International Symposium on Wearable Computing (UbiComp/IWSC), Oct. 13 in Shanghai. Credit: Provided Saif Mahmud, a Ph.D. candidate in the field of information science, demonstrates EchoMotion, a system for tracking body movements using an off-the-shelf smartwatch. “This is a very important jump for body tracking,” said Saif Mahmud, doctoral student in the field of information science and lead author of the new research. Existing wearable devices use sensors such as accelerometers and gyroscopes that determine the movement of the device alone, he said. As a result, whole body tracking traditionally has required more complicated setups that may also include smartphones, earbuds or VR headsets. Some tracking systems also integrate cameras, but EchoMotion’s use of sound waves offers multiple advantages. Acoustic signals preserve privacy for the wearer and the people around them – no need to set up a camera at the gym – and generate smaller amounts of data for easier and cheaper processing. “While large language models, like ChatGPT, have been in the news, EchoMotion shows how very small models running on wearables have also revolutionized sensing in human-computer interaction,” said co-author  François Guimbretière , professor of information science in Cornell Bowers. The technology also saves on battery power and works with existing off-the-shelf watches. In the prototype, sensing drew about 12 milliwatts, roughly 40 times less than a wearable camera, and a 30-minute session on a Galaxy Watch 6 used only 5% to 6% of the battery. “We have made significant efforts in making EchoMotion work on commercial devices, so that the adoption can be very easy,” Mahmud said. To develop the technology, the researchers initially created their own 3D-printed watch replica, which included a microphone and speaker pair on each side. The two speakers emit ultrasonic signals that surround a person in a sphere of inaudible sound waves. Then the two microphones pick up the echoes that bounce off the person’s limbs as they move. The researchers collected echo patterns from 10 volunteers who wore the watch on their nondominant hand as they performed 18 exercises. Using that data, the researchers developed a deep learning model to translate those patterns into body movements. They measured accuracy by comparing the predicted positions of 12 joints, from head to ankles, with the body poses captured by cameras. Off-the-shelf smartwatches have only a single microphone and speaker pair, however, so they tested the EchoMotion system on an unmodified Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 with 15 new volunteers. When used by people new to the system, the average error for predicting the location of each joint was under four inches. A one-time, 12-minute calibration cut that error by more than one third, to about 2.4 inches. The same AI model, without any retraining, also worked on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3. To see how EchoMotion performed beyond the lab, the researchers asked 10 new participants to wear a smartwatch as they did the 18 exercises in a small room, in a narrow hallway and next to a noisy road. Furniture and ambient noise did not interfere, but the system’s performance suffered slightly in the hallway, due to echoes coming off of other people. Mahmud expects, however, that with more data – from thousands of users instead of dozens – their model will get better at interpreting a wearer’s movements even in crowded environments, like the subway. Currently, the team is developing the technology for use in fitness tracking, so a personal fitness agent will be able to count a user’s reps and even correct their form, for example, in a Bulgarian split squat. They are also exploring the use of EchoMotion in combination with first-person vision on smartglasses to efficiently track the objects that a person handles. “In the very near future, with wearables like smartwatches or smartglasses, a personal agent will write a description of your whole day – what you did, what you ate,” Mahmud said. “This project enables the body tracking part of that vision.” Co-authors on the study include Jiwan Kim of KAIST; Tianhong Catherine Yu, a doctoral student in the field of information science; Kenny Liang ’24 and Vineet Parikh ’20, M.S. ’24. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation. Patricia Waldron is a writer for the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science.
