title: Windows 11 is collecting data on which coding agents and developer tools you use
body_text: Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use :: Xusheng Li > Xusheng Blog Contact CV CVEs Media Coverage Research 7 minutes Windows 11 Is Collecting Data on Which Coding Agents and Developer Tools You Use Reverse engineering Windows 11's MissionControlAggregator reveals coding-agent and developer-tool usage bits in a diagnostic ETW report. I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe , claude.exe , copilot.exe , and cursor.exe , alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe , dotnet.exe , gcc.exe , and code.exe . Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools? The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll . I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft. I shared the initial finding on X . This post includes more details about the investigation behind it. Following the names Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component: Following the references showed that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe , claude.exe , codex.exe , and agy.exe , with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe , claude.exe , codex.exe , cursor.exe , and antigravity.exe . Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe : The compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers . For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<<lambda_340dfe7e962ab225b6ac33bc664bd54f>, bool, std::basic_string_view<wchar_t, std::char_traits<wchar_t>> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call . The screenshot shows another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison. The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage , feature ID 62580080 . And the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe , python.exe , dotnet.exe , gcc.exe , clang.exe , gdb.exe , javac.exe , devenv.exe , and code.exe , among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation , Python expects Python Software Foundation , and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation . The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path. Where does the DLL get this information? The next question was whether the component scans running processes itself. Following Aggregator::OnLoad revealed that it subscribes to existing Windows events instead. For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary . These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical , using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL. The relevant flow looks like this: Aggregator::OnLoad ├─ WSL Exec / ExecCritical │ └─ ProcessWslExecEvent → CLI agent matchers ├─ KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary │ └─ ProcessAppStateChangeSummaryEvent → CLI agent matchers └─ Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary └─ ProcessAppInteractivitySummaryEvent → desktop agent matchers Aggregator::OnRelativeTimerExpire └─ MissionControlAggregatorLogging::ReportCohorts<12,4,5> └─ Segments.SubCohorts ETW report Aggregator::OnUnload / intermediate timer └─ PersistentState::SaveToDisk A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts . The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents. ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window. The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used. Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications. Is it actually running on a normal machine? Strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974 . Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818 , and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature. DiagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic . It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module: PS> Get-Service DiagTrack | Format-Table Name,Status,StartType -AutoSize Name Status StartType ---- ------ --------- DiagTrack Running Automatic PS> Get-Process AggregatorHost | Format-Table ProcessName,Id -AutoSize ProcessName Id ----------- -- AggregatorHost 1500 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='DiagTrack'" | Format-List Name,State,StartMode,ProcessId Name : DiagTrack State : Running StartMode : Auto ProcessId : 10148 PS> Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter "Name='AggregatorHost.exe'" | Format-List ProcessId,ParentProcessId ProcessId : 1500 ParentProcessId : 10148 PS> tasklist /m MissionControlAggregator.dll Image Name PID Modules ========================= ======== ============================================ AggregatorHost.exe 1500 MissionControlAggregator.dll The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148 , which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe , process 1500 ; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child. Testing it in practice To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex. I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ( {2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f} ), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0 . The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection. That state is persisted in: C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Diagnosis\AggregatorStorage\MissionControlAggregator$ The report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained: Provider: Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator Time: 2026-11-16T12:34:29.125116Z Version: 0.1.5 CliAgentSubCohorts: 4 DesktopAgentSubCohorts: 0 FlushedFromSave: true The value 4 is 1 << 2 : the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report. I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe . It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] ( 1 << 3 ). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable. Following the report toward Microsoft An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report. The VM already had a Diagtrack-Listener session subscribed to both ends of the path. These PowerShell queries showed its subscriptions: Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener ` -Guid '{2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}' Get-EtwTraceProvider -SessionName Diagtrack-Listener ` -Guid '{00de11a2-ec06-58e5-1a2b-21bb21dbee4b}' The first subscription, for KernelProcess , had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002 , which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator , had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000 , which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255 . The subscription showed where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data . When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue: { "name" : "Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator.Segments.SubCohorts" , "ext" : { "privacy" : { "isRequired" : false } }, "data" : { "Version" : "0.1.5" , "CliAgentSubCohorts" : [ 4 ], "DesktopAgentSubCohorts" : [ 0 ], "FlushedFromSave" : true } } I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the Diagnostic data toggle was already enabled and labeled Include Optional . After completing setup with those defaults, AllowTelemetry was 3 , confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled. Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off Send optional diagnostic data later under Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback . Microsoft’s diagnostics and privacy guide explains how to change it. title: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker
body_text: Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker iter.ca â¢ About â¢ Uses â¢ Accounts â¢ Notes Universal XSS in uBlock Origin from website-driven element picker By Smitty van Bodegom (loops) Â· Nov 15, 2026 Earlier this month I found a one-click universal XSS issue with uBlock Origin (the MV2 Firefox version, although a similar but less problematic issue also affected the MV3 version, uBO Lite), where a malicious website could trick the extension into adding arbitrary trusted filters. Trusted filters can inject JavaScript code into pages, and so the malicious website could create a trusted filter on another website and run arbitrary JS in the context of any site. This issue is fixed now; you can read the GitHub advisory for some more details. GPT-5.6 Sol did most of the hard work of finding the issue. I figured there might be some kind of UXSS from filter injection, so I asked it to take a look, and it found the issue. I then checked and verified the issue it proposed. I wrote all of the prose in this post myself; Claude wrote most of the code for the PoC. The issue uBlock Origin has an element picker that you can pull up by right-clicking on the page. You can use this to create a filter rule to block an element on the page without leaving the page. The element picker is implemented by injecting an iframe to a URL like moz-extension://76b2331a-894c-4d25-8b89-fcce37e79cc4/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html . That page can talk to the extension background script and tell it to add filters. Basically the attack here is: Figure out the element picker URL Create our own invisible (opacity 0) iframe that embeds it Drive the picker to put the filter we want in it Position the invisible iframe to trick the user into pressing the invisible “Create” button Figuring out the element picker URL On Firefox, the only information we needed to figure out was the extension internal UUID which is random per-installation. On the default setup uBO has a lootdest.*##+js(no-fetch-if, adsbygoogle, war:googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js) filter rule (from uAssets), which hooks fetch . From inside the fetch hook, it makes an XHR request to moz-extension://<extension UUID>/web_accessible_resources/googlesyndication_adsbygoogle.js and returns the response from that as the fetch body, instead of actually making the request. The filter rule is intended to replace a network request for JS from an ad server with a dummy script that has the correct API but doesn’t do anything. But the attacker website can itself hook the XHR made from inside the no-fetch-if hook to extract the random extension UUID. const origOpen = XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open ; XMLHttpRequest . prototype . open = function ( m , url , ... a ) { const e = /^moz-extension:\/\/[^/]+/ . exec ( url ); if ( e ) { e [ 0 ] // <- has the extension UUID! } return origOpen . call ( this , m , url , ... a ); }; Then the attacker website can run fetch('/adsbygoogle.js').catch(() => {}); to trigger the filter, and make their hooked XHR run. Note that there are several ways that the extension internal UUID could be leaked; it’s not just this one filter rule. Creating an iframe Then you can use that to iframe the element picker. Given an iframe element in the page, you just set its src to `moz-extension://${origin}/web_accessible_resources/epicker-ui.html` . Sending messages to it Now we can drive the element picker. We can create a MessageChannel and do iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ what: 'epickerStart' }, '*', [ch.port2]); to send it to the picker iframe. Then we talk to it: it sends us a start message, we send it a showDialog message with a filter and a resultsetDetails message 1 to enable the create button and set opt . Normally the picker restricts what filters you can enter, and doesn’t let you add scriptlet filters. But there’s a trick we can do to add arbitrary filters. There’s an opt field we set in the second message which is normally the type of network request to match (like image ), and gets appended to the filter with a $ if set, like $image . But since we control it, we can put a newline in it and make it "image\ngoogle.com##+js(trusted-rpnt, script, ...)" to inject an arbitrary trusted filter that injects a script. 2 This is where the main issue is - the element picker shouldn’t accept messages from the attacker. One of the fixes was having a secret password that the real element picker gets from the content script, that the element picker sends in the initial postMessage. Getting the click I didn’t bother actually implementing this, but malicious websites could overlay stuff on top of the embedded element picker or make it invisible by setting the iframe opacity to 0. So as long as the website can get the user to click on the page, it can add arbitrary trusted filters for arbitrary domains. Filters added by the element picker are always treated as trusted (at least until a recompile), which is why it can add a trusted filter. If the user later changes their custom filters it would cause a recompile, clearing the filter trust. But in practice the attacker could just immediately open the victim webpage, so this doesn’t help much. Originally I sent that message in reply to a dialogSetFilter message from the picker, but it turns out you can just send it right away instead of waiting to reply.  ↩︎ Assuming the shown filter is a network filter.  ↩︎ Related Bypassing the GitHub workflow permission with nested Git tags Malleating Git commit signatures Forging signed commits on GitHub Don't run your own mailserver Patching protobufs poetically X: @_smitop ð§ m e&#x000000000000000000000000000000040;it er.c a Discord: @moreloops Content license: CC-BY-SA 4.0 Tags: security programming Comments Subscribe to my occasional email newsletter:

title: Rust changed me as a developer
body_text: Secret Weblog • How Rust Changed Me As A Developer 🫥 '> Secret Weblog blog archive tags How Rust Changed Me As A Developer By Martijn Faassen  •  2026-11-16  •  Tags:  programming ,  rust How Rust Changed Me As A Developer The programming language you use affects how you think as a software developer 1 . That may seem surprising to you; you may have picked up JavaScript pretty quickly knowing Python, and it didn't really affect how you think or develop. That's because those languages are pretty similar. The more different a programming language is from what you're used to, the more it can change you. Rust was quite different to me, so it did. I've been developing with Rust for over 6 years; more than 4 years professionally now . One of the reasons I really wanted to become more proficient with Rust is because I knew it would challenge me, and hopefully change me for the better as a developer. I think it did. What I learned and am going to discuss here is not exclusive to Rust. You can encounter many of these concepts in other contexts, and indeed I had encountered quite a few of them already. But in this case, Rust helped bring them into better focus. Where were enums all my life? We're all familiar with product types, though not usually under that name: struct Human { first_name : String, last_name : String, } The fields of the Human struct 2 can vary independently from each other, and we have to deal with all possible combinations: all possible first names and last names, combined. The product of their combinations, to to speak. But it turns out there's another type thing that's been around forever but that the programming community has mostly been been ignoring 3 : the sum type. A sum type expresses variants: something is either one thing, or another, out of a bunch of variants: enum Person { Human { first_name: String , last_name: String }, Cat { name: String , cuteness: Cuteness } } A Person is either a human or a cat: that's the sum of the possiblities. Each variant can have data associated with it, and this can be a product type, but the Person type is just these options (two in this case). In code where you need to deal with a person, you need to handle each variant by match in on the object. The Rust compiler enforces this. match some_person { Human { first_name, last_name } => { // do a thing with first_name and last_name }, Cat { name, cuteness } => { // do a thing with name and cutenes } } When you handle the human variant, you only need to worry about first_name and last_name . You don't have to worry about name or cuteness at all. These cases are distinct from each other. It turns out that it's really helpful to model stuff using sum types. People using functional programming languages already knew this. You can model optionality ( null ) this way: you got either some value, or nothing. You can also model errors: it's either okay (with whatever value you return in case of success), or an error (with a value describing the error). Any language without sum types now feels impoverished to me. I know I can simulate it with some type field, but the job of a programming language is to help me handle basic stuff, and this is basic stuff. Enums and abstraction In an object oriented programming language, you handle variants using dynamic dispatch and an interface (or inheritance). You do this: interface Person { def do_one_thing() def do_another_thing } class Human implements Person { ... } class Cat implements Person { ... } The idea is that you can now use Person anywhere without worrying about the details inside: it's loosely coupled. You only use their interface. This is indeed a great idea, but Rust taught me that this has tradeoffs I may not want to pay for. You pay two things: performance, and the need to create the interface. Let's talk about the need to create the interface. You need to devise an interface that actually makes sense for your application: how are you using humans and cats everywhere? Doing this work of abstraction may be extremely worthwhile to do, especially if you anticipate unknown future persons that you need to be able to plug in later without having to modify the code that uses them -- you want your code use the open/closed principle . But what if you are developing a single domain, and inside that you just want to be able to handle cats and humans and that's it? There's just no need to plug in other types of persons, and certainly not from outside. Or let's say you do want to add a new variant once every while. Say you want to add Dog . Maybe you're actually okay going through the code that handles Human and Cat and add handling for dogs too? Maybe it actually is helpful to see those other handlers right there too when you do so? The compiler is going to ensure you don't miss any spots! Or what if the abstraction you are trying to devise is the variance and that's more or less what you can say about it? For error handling, the abstraction is either okay with some value, or some error value. In this case you may be paying the price of creating an interface without it being worthwhile. enum may be all you actually need -- low ceremony, and statically checked. Finally I'll note that enums don't lock you out from creating that abstraction - you can add methods to an enum too, just like on a struct. Enums made me a better programmer as now I have another elementary, simple, easy to understand language construct for abstraction in my mental toolbox. Dispatch galore In many languages there are two types of dispatch: dynamic dispatch, which we've discussed in case of our Person interface, and conditional dispatch, like this: if something { do_this_thing() } else do_another() } Rust has dynamic dispatch, if you ask for it. It also has the powered up version of conditional dispatch I already discussed: match on enums. It has conditional dispatch too - that's just [a special case][https://docs.rs/bool/latest/bool/enum.Boolean.html]. There's another type of dispatch that Rust makes you think about: dispatch that's statically compiled. What if you're dealing either with groups of humans or groups of cats, and you want to do some operations on them, and those operations have common behavior (say, you want to count them). The group, or collection, doesn't really care about what's in it, as long as every item fulfills certain basic properties. You could create an enum Person ; either an enum or an interface with multiple implementations, and then dispatch during runtime to every member of the group based on whether that entry is a human or a cat. But this means you have to account for mixed groups of humans and cats, even though we just said those don't actually exist. Instead, you can express this differently in Rust. You still have a Person interface (trait), but you compose your individual type of Person ( Human or Cat ) during compile time. struct Group <T> { // some fields } // compile time assembly, // then runtime creation of the assembled group of cats let cat_group: Group<Cat> = Group::new(); Rust now refuses to compile if you use non-cat operations on items in the group, That's an invariant you now do not need to worry about anymore. This will be familiar to you with generics in other languages like TypeScript or Python. In Rust, when you process your group of cats, there is no individual check somewhere whether an entry is a human or a cat, as it already knows it's all cats before the program even ran. Rust directly dispatches to the cat code, and the human code is not play. You avoid indirect dispatch for every group member, which can matter in situations where performance is important. Rust made me a better programmer as I now better understand the connection between dispatch and performance. Type driven development When I discovered Python coming from C++ back in the late 1990s, dynamic typing was a revelation. You could so much with so little ceremony. For the last decade or so I have been on a long winding road back to types (far more ergonomic types) and more ceremony. I have the impression many have been on this journey along with me 4 . Types can statically check your code before it runs. In Rust, they can help the compiler compile stuff down to really high performance code. Both are great. But types can also have more subtle benefits. Let me get into this by analogy. Why create automated tests? Obvious : Automated tests ensure various properties of your code work and remain working. Subtle : Writing tests forces you to think about the architecture and APIs you're implementing more carefully. Making code testable can lead to better architecture. This is the insight of test driven development. Why write documentation? Obvious : People (and now machines) can understand 5 the why and what of your software by reading the documentation. Subtle : The act of writing the documentation can force you think about the architecture and APIs of your software. If you can't write about it, maybe you haven't gotten it right yet? That's documentation driven development. Why write types? Obvious : Statically check your code before it runs! Prevent runtime errors! Performance! Subtle : You model the domain model using types, trying to make sure it hangs together. Enums are really valuable here. You express parse, don't validate in them. The types guide the architecture and APIs of your software. This perhaps sounds like big design up front processes where people write all the tests, or all the docs, or all the types, in advance, and then do the implementation. 6 I'm not talking about this -- I'm talking about iterative development where you keep going back to tests, docs and types as you learn. Rust brought into focus how types are yet another tool to help me think while I develop. Rust made me a better programmer as it let me fully embrace type driven development. The Biggest Surprise Here is the biggest surprise I had coming to Rust. Much of the behavior I associated with dynamic interpreted languages with a rich runtime like Python can actually be done statically in Rust using macros. Let's talk about magic. Say you want to dump the state of a Python object -- you inspect all its fields, look at their type, turn each into a string, combine all the strings together into a big one. Now you can store it somewhere. Later on you restore that string back into an object. You can save and load any objects: magic! Python calls this pickle . What if you need to serialize to JSON? Python has a type system, and a library like Pydantic inspects the type objects during runtime and then uses this information to let you automatically serialize a Python object to JSON, or parse it back into Python again. More magic! Rust is a compiled language. Types aren't runtime objects. Without reflection, which takes special effort , runtime introspection of types is not a thing in Rust. But Rust can still do what Pickle and Pydantic do, at compile time. With serde , Rust's answer to pickle and Pydantic, you use a normal Rust type, annotate it with a few declarations, and then you can serialize it to JSON, or toml config format, and many other formats, and load it back again. The annotation looks like this: #[ derive (Serialize, Deserialize)] struct Human { first_name : String, last_name : String } With clap , you create the type that expresses exactly what command line arguments you expect (with enum s too!), document it using the normal way you document any API in Rust, and boom, you have a CLI with built in help. The code that handles the various cases gets well-typed data - at that point it's been parsed correctly already, using the same type you used to express the CLI. Like this: /// My first CLI #[ derive (Parser)] struct MyFirstCli { /// How many cats do you want? #[ arg (long, short)] amount_of_cats : usize } Again declarative #[] stuff going on. It looks a lot like decorators in Python. But Python decorators are executed during runtime, and we just said Rust doesn't normally let you do that. How does that work in Rust? Macros! Macros lets you write code that generates code during compile time. With serde, the macro generates a whole bunch of serialization code and deserialization code for the types annotated with it. This generated code gets compiled along with the rest of your code. The compiler can optimize it just like any other code. Code generation is scary. Macros are scary. Doing introspection in a dynamically typed language is a lot easier than using Rust macros, where code is parsed and generated. Macros shouldn't be randomly mixed with application code; macros belong in frameworks. That said, something being easy doesn't mean it should be used casually: in Python you typically want to carefully encapsulate your magic in a declarative framework too. Rust made me a better programmer as I learned about a new class of framework patterns. Ownership and Architecture Rust famously lets you write code without memory leaks that doesn't use a garbage collector. It also stops you from mutating data you're also reading elsewhere, making it impossible to stumble into whole classes of weird undefined behavior, especially with code that runs in parallel. Rust's ownership system is one of the main things that makes learning Rust hard. Python, JavaScript, Java and many other languages have mutable references everywhere, and you can just create cyclic data structures. Rust won't let you do either out of the box. The equivalent of this does not compile in Rust: class Item : def __init__ ( self , value ): self .value = value class Container : def __init__ ( self , items ): self .items = items my_item = Item() my_container = Container() my_container.items.append(my_item) my_item.value = "I change you!" This also doesn't compile: class Node : def __init__ ( self , parent , value ): self .parent = parent self .value = value self .children = [] def add_child ( self , node ): node.parent = self self.children.append(node) Rust won't just let you have circular references, in this case both children and a parent reference. This feels very limiting at first! What do you do instead? For mutating stuff, you learn how to separate mutation (often during construction) from using your data. That is a thing that's good to do in many contexts -- less invariants makes it's easier to reason about, but it takes a bit of getting used to Rust strictly enforcing it. For circular references it's trickier. I will go into it next, when I discuss arenas. A weird thing happens: if you lean into this friction it can improve the architecture of your codebase. Code becomes less coupled. It's hard to create weird backchannels with action at a distance that makes code difficult to understand, test and debug 7 . Rust code locally can be difficult to understand. But how the data flows, what does what, in the larger codebase, tends to be cleaner. Rust made me a better programmer as I now think about ownership more carefully, which has a positive impact on architecture. The arena pattern everywhere A few years ago I analyzed a bunch of XML tree libraries in Rust. The best I found, roxmltrree , has an immutable tree. But I needed a mutable tree. I found quite a few libraries that did support mutability, but many did not support parent references. You couldn't walk up the ancestor chain of a node. This, along with missing support for some XML features, is why I created my own in the form of Xot . The reason for this surprising lack of parent references is the ownership limitation I discussed before: Rust makes circular references difficult. You can get around it using reference counted types and internal mutability, but in a lot of cases this pattern isn't really optimal -- it's verbose, less performant, and reference count cycles risk memory leaks. What you do instead is store nodes in an array and you use the array indexes to node as your reference. You can then have an index referencing your parent, and use index references to your children, or any other circular reference. A fancy word for this pattern is an 'arena' and in Rust they show up everywhere. In an arena, you store a lot of objects together in the same region of memory (in an array). What does it let you do? iterate fast over its contents. Objects being in the same memory region means the CPU can use its cache effectively. This is much faster than arbitrary main memory access and loops really benefit. fast allocation. The arena is allocated from the heap as a block, and after that your allocations may just be a few increments. interning: you store something once in the arena and use it in many places, so you don't duplicate data. the arena owns its stuff. Everything in the arena has the same lifetime. Indexes between objects in an arena can be circular without worrying. Rust pushes you to use arenas. This involves more ceremony than just using a direct reference, but it also means Rust pushes you to write code that computers can execute really efficiently. Performance has a quality all its own I mentioned performance a number of times. But what about premature optimization ? The great irony of this quote is that it comes from a paper where the author, Knuth, argues in favor of keeping the goto statement around, as it's essential for writing efficient software. Rust lets you know what you pay for. Reference counting? Dynamic dispatch? You can do it, but it's going to be visible in your code. Rust also often lets you know when you don't want to pay for it: just look at tower middleware and despair about all the generic types and type constraints that get piled onto a relatively simple abstraction. When you have these tools available, need to develop new wisdom about tradeoffs that never seemed to matter. If you write Python code you're not too worried about hash tables being a performance bottle neck, but in Rust code they certainly can be. You can get lost along the way into hyper optimization land. Often you need to just get go 8 . Many patterns that are just plain readable Rust code anyway happen to also be friendly to the CPU executing it. But Rust overwhelming you with details you may not want to think about is not the whole story, because performance is not just quantitative: if your code can truly be more performance, it can access new qualities. When you can write code that uses no memory and no CPU time 9 , it changes how you think. It changes what's possible. Sometimes the quality of performance is obvious: if you write numerical code, or a simulation, of course you don't want to wait for the answer. Being able to do many computations really fast is key to making AI possible. But it's more subtle that that: modern computers are really powerful, and ridicously fast, and we generally ignore that and just throw more resources at our problems. There are good reasons why this happens . But if we open our eyes a little, there are new architectural possibilities we can explore. While the power of macros were the biggest language surprise, I think this is the biggest shift in my thinking: access to performance unlocks possibilities I hadn't considered before. Take my experiment Colchis : a library can store vast amounts of JSON in memory, while retaining full access, even indexed access (I still hope to add jsonpath one day!), to JSON data. Before Rust, this was a possibility that wasn't even on my radar. Rust made me a better programmer because I can make the computer do more with less, opening up new areas of opportunity. Conclusion Rust is one of the most difficult programming languages I've learned -- and thus one of the languages that changed me the most. There's a simple part of Rust that isn't much harder to manage than any language, and in some cases may actually make your life easier -- enum s, declarative type-driven frameworks, and the excellent dev tooling come to mind. Even arenas are fundamentally not that difficult to understand. The complexity is in unlearning some habits and learning new ones. And then there's a more challenging complex Rust, mostly, but not always under the surface, there when you need it. Rust expands the reach of what I can build. That's what makes me happy I went on this journey. 10 1 AI agents write a lot of code. They know the programming language, so do you need to know it? Does the language still affect the developer? If you share my belief it's good to look at the code , then it helps if you understand the code you're reading. I also think it's never been more important to think about how the systems you use affect the way you think and behave. 2 If you don't know what a struct is, just call it a class in your head, and you're good. 3 You have them in many languages but in impoverished forms, like true / false , or C's enum . 4 If you're going to do static type checking anyway for the guarantees it brings, perhaps use a language designed around it (enums!) that also gives you performance benefits? 5 Does AI truly understand? Do you want to have a philosophical debate? What do we mean by understand ? Natural language is inherently stretchable . 6 With AI we've seen the return of big design up front. I may be wrong, but I'm still skeptical of this approach, and still a fan of iterative development and incremental learning and theory building. 7 Not impossible. I've seen it. People can do it if they really try, and it still makes life harder; it makes it much harder to test. But at least it's more obvious and more difficult to do. 8 Clone and own all the stuff! Which incidentally can also lead to more contiguous memory layouts... 9 No memory and no CPU time is an exaggeration, but little Rust programs sometimes feel that way. 10 AI development is shifting all the tradeoffs in software development - they're not gone, but they have shifted. The AI can write Rust, even if you don't know it. But I trust plenty of contexts remain where my Rust experience plus AI leads to a better outcome than AI by itself. ←  Prev Coding with a Sigh Copied! title: The Secret ThinkPad Powerbutton Code to Bring Dead Laptops Back to Life (2007)
body_text: The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life | Mike Masnick Mike Masnick Blog About Search Techdirt   The Secret Thinkpad Powerbutton Code To Bring Dead Laptops Back To Life Mike Masnick · September 7, 2007 Permalink Two months ago, I got a new laptop. It’s a Lenovo Thinkpad z61t. I actually ordered a t61, but I accidentally got the z61 instead — and, I actually really like it. It’s quite similar to the t61, but a little smaller and lighter. I was worried that the smaller part would be a problem, but I’ve gotten used to it. I really like the fact that it’s much lighter than my old t42. It just makes it seem so much more usable on the go. Lugging out the t42 was always a chore. Anyway, I was at the Office 2.0 conference today, where I was giving a little presentation on the Techdirt Insight Community, and about an hour before the presentation, I went to find a quiet place to practice the presentation… and discovered that my brand new laptop wouldn’t work. I knew something was wrong when the “sleep” light wasn’t lit. I started to get worried when I plugged in the laptop and the battery light didn’t light up. Then I noticed that even though the machine had been asleep, it was really really hot. Pushing the power button did nothing. No lights were on and nothing seemed to get them to turn on. I pulled out the battery and put it back in and that did nothing as well. So I called up IBM support and explained the situation. The guy on the other end then let me in on the secret power button code to revive your dead Thinkpad. After assessing the situation (totally dead laptop) he warned me: “Okay, this is going to sound totally bizarre, but I want you to give this a try…” He then had me unplug the AC adapter and take out the battery. Then, you push the power button 10 times in a row at one second intervals. Next, you push and hold the power button for 30 seconds. Then you put the battery back in and push the power button… and she lives. The computer came back, good as ever. I asked the guy what the power button pushing incantation did and he said “static discharge” so apparently there was some sort of static that caused a short or something. I tried to get the guy to explain in more detail what happened, but he said “dude, you know as much as I do… but your machine is working.” And so it is. So, if you happen to have a Thinkpad that suddenly drops completely dead for no reason, try the power button trick. Forget up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A. This isn’t a magic trick, the point of this besides the static discharge, this resets the Bios of computer by pulling all the charge out of the Internal 2032 CMOS Battery, which in return reboots the BIOS. This can happen for many reason not just a static charge, Some computers can have a bad infection that activates when the computer goes to sleep mode, this is a well known attacker, then the virus proceeds to overload your machine to shut down thus causing the bios to have the command programmed to stay shut down. Well by doing the manual BIOS RESET such as this, resets the configurations in the bios back to default. Also you can try pulling battery out, unplugging charger, and then hold power button for 1 minute if the 10X an 30sec hold doesn’t work for you. And if for some reason it still don’t work, removing the 2032 CMOS Battery on the MOBO for 1 minute or replace it, the battery which is usually located near the RAM on most laptops, not all have the battery located in same place, I suggest if you need to go that far google your model of computer to locate the internal CMOS Battery. data-display-video-cover="true" data-details=""> Pilot announces systems are back online after United Airlines widespread system outage 0:19 • Source: CNN Pilot announces systems are back online after United Airlines widespread system outage 0:19 Federal agencies Air travel safety Aviation news See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Follow A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at US airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruption . The outage lasted about 30 minutes, with fewer than 150 flights impacted, United Airlines spokesperson Leslie Scott told CNN. United acknowledged the issue just before 5 p.m. ET, saying the technology outage was impacting departing flights, and an hour later the airline announced it had been resolved. “While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,” United Airlines said in a statement. During the incident, the FAA said United was experiencing a technology outage on its end and that “it’s not an FAA equipment issue.” Related article CNN ‘Working on floppy disks’: FAA has fielded years of warnings about old systems 7 min read United said there is no indication that the outage was a cybersecurity-related issue. The technology outage affected access to multiple applications used by flight crews, according to an internal company alert obtained by CNN. The airline instructed pilots not to log out of several systems, warning they may be unable to sign back in. The affected applications included flight planning, weather briefing and crew management tools. Pilots unable to access their flight plans were being directed to contact dispatchers to have the documents emailed to them. The memo did not disclose the cause of the outage. Air traffic control audio captured by ATC.com shows the moment the outage occurred. “Hey, we’re uh, still waiting on our final weights,” a pilot on United Flight 1728 in El Paso, heading to Denver, said to a controller. “We just contacted ops and apparently there’s a company-wide system outage on it so might be a while.” The controller responds back, “United 1728, roger, so you don’t have any idea when you think you’ll be able to leave?” “No ma’am,” the pilot responds. Aviation industry still recovering from weekend ground stop The industry had largely returned to normal operations after the nationwide ground stop was lifted just after 8 p.m. ET on Friday, though airlines have still worked to reposition planes, crews and luggage as they grappled with the weekend’s score of cancellations and delays . Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy held a 45-minute news conference Saturday morning to address the FAA ground stop, and apologized to travelers as he said he was still working to determine what exactly went wrong. Related article A traveler waits in line at John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York on November 14. Ryan Murphy/Getty Images With the busiest travel season ahead, how likely is it that another FAA ground stop happens? 8 min read Duffy told reporters that upgrade work on an old telecommunication system could be a cause for Friday’s nationwide ground stop. In at least one remote FAA location, Duffy said contractor L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from an old copper wire to fiber, which he described as “straightforward” work that has been happening across the country for decades. As United Airlines indicated for Monday’s system outage, Friday’s ground stop didn’t appear to have been caused by a cyber attack or any “nefarious” activity, Duffy stressed at the news conference. “A lot of questions came in yesterday. ‘Was this a, a cyber attack? Did some foreign nation attack this network?’ And the answer to that is we don’t believe so,” Duffy said. This story has been updated with additional information. title: Chinese frontier AI models carry the fingerprint of export-controlled GPUs
body_text: Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs · Unemployment Labs Skip to report Unemployment Labs In this report Executive summary Main findings Our investigation Limits of the investigation Verifying the findings Conclusion Appendix 1 · Lab histories Appendix 2 · All models Sources How to cite Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs Will DePue November 12, 2026 Print / save PDF Cite this report Executive Summary Our forensic analysis of publicly released AI models finds evidence that DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to NVIDIA’s Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models. Six models released by these companies since April 2026 contain numerical patterns matching Blackwell hardware, whereas earlier models from the same companies match NVIDIA’s older Hopper generation. The findings suggest that several leading Chinese AI developers have begun using Blackwell to train their newest models. U.S. officials and press reports had already alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, without publishing technical evidence. The evidence comes entirely from the models’ own published weights, rather than from leaks or insider accounts. We recover traces of the models’ initial values, and then search for the hardware configurations and initial configurations that reproduce them; for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, we also confirmed the match on physical Blackwell chips. The fingerprint identifies how the weights were created and supports, without proving, the inference that Blackwell also performed the training. Specially configured AMD hardware, which is also restricted from export to China, is the only alternative we have identified; we have excluded it for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and consider it very unlikely for the other five models. Notably, our findings provide technical evidence of access to advanced computing hardware, but do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. Table 1. Hardware fingerprints in successive models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group Link ↗ Lab Model Released Chip the model was started on DeepSeek DeepSeek-V3 Dec 2024 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) DeepSeek-V4-Flash Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 DeepSeek-V4-Pro Apr 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Moonshot AI Kimi K2 Jul 2025 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K2.5 Jan 2026 NVIDIA Hopper (lab disclosed H800) Kimi K3 Jul 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 Kimi K3.1-Pro Nov 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 MiniMax MiniMax-M2.7 Apr 2026 NVIDIA Hopper MiniMax-M3 Jun 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell B200/B300 Ant Group Ling-3.0-flash Aug 2026 NVIDIA Hopper Ling-3.1-flash Oct 2026 • NVIDIA Blackwell GB200/GB300 • Requires a U.S. license for export to China; none have been reported. A Hopper fingerprint cannot distinguish an H800 from an H100 SXM or H200; the H800 identifications above are lab disclosures, not findings of this method. Full list of models in Appendix 2 ↓ Main Findings Six models from four Chinese labs read as Blackwell-trained. DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match NVIDIA’s Blackwell-class B200 or B300 chips, which have 148 processor cores (called streaming multiprocessors , or SMs). DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ling-3.1-flash match the GB200 or GB300 chips, also Blackwell-class, which have 152 processor cores. Kimi K3.1-Pro starts from the same seed as K3, and may be a checkpoint of K3 with further post-training. Chinese labs started training on Blackwell relatively recently. DeepSeek’s models read as Hopper-trained through DeepSeek-V3 (released in December 2024), and as Blackwell from DeepSeek V4 (released in April 2026). Moonshot’s models read as Hopper through Kimi K2.5 (January 2026) and as Blackwell from K3 (July 2026). One Moonshot model sits in between: Kimi K2.7-Code, posted six weeks before K3, is built on the Hopper-era weights but contains a small part that matches the B200 or B300. MiniMax’s models read as Hopper through M2.7 (April 2026) and as Blackwell from M3 (June 2026). Ant Group’s Ling-3.0-flash (August 2026) reads as Hopper, while its Ling-3.1-flash (October 2026) reads as Blackwell. The Hopper readings do not identify a specific chip: H800s, H100 SXMs and H200s share the same fingerprint. Not every Chinese AI lab has switched to Blackwell. The newest models we could read from Alibaba (Qwen), Zhipu (GLM), Tencent, Xiaomi and StepFun all read as Hopper-trained. Meituan says its LongCat-2.0 was trained entirely on “AI ASIC superpods,” and we found no NVIDIA fingerprint in the model weights it’s released. The method gets known answers right. For 24 specific models, the developer has publicly said what hardware was used. In every case, our method agrees with the public announcement. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of its training, reads as 152 SMs, the same as Kimi K3. The matches are far stronger than chance would explain. Even unrelated numbers can appear to match when enough combinations are tried. Across the roughly 6 trillion seed-and-layout combinations in our search, the strongest chance match would be expected to reach about 8 sigma—a measure of how far a result stands above ordinary random variation. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma. Even the weakest individual test we report reaches 20 sigma. The training runs were data-center scale. From each model’s size and the amount of data it was trained on, we estimate that the two largest runs, Kimi K3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro, each needed thousands of Blackwell GPUs for two to three months, assuming each model was trained on the hardware that initialized it. Our best estimates are about 4,500 and 3,000, the equivalent of about 11,500 and 7,500 H100s, the previous-generation NVIDIA chip in which AI training clusters are commonly sized, and about 12,000 Blackwell GPUs across the five runs (Table 2). Our investigation A model’s weights , also called parameters , are the billions of adjustable numbers that determine how it processes information and produces answers. Training repeatedly adjusts these numbers; but before training can begin, they need initial values. In the software examined here, those values come from a pseudorandom number generation (PRNG) algorithm called Philox: Philox produces seemingly random numbers in a deterministic way. The starting input for Philox is a number called the “seed.” Given the same seed and settings, Philox produces the same numbers every time. This lets engineers repeat an experiment from the same starting point. To fill billions of weights quickly, PyTorch, the software framework used in the development of most major AI models, divides the work that Philox does among many parallel workers on the GPU, called threads . (It does this through cuRAND, NVIDIA’s library for random number generation.) Each thread generates its own sequence of numbers from the seed and fills a particular set of positions. The number of threads then determines how those positions are shared out. On the NVIDIA chips examined here, a sufficiently large initialization uses the maximum of 2,048 threads for each processing unit, called a streaming multiprocessor (SM). A chip with more SMs therefore assigns the same job to more workers, changing where their numbers go. Figure 1 illustrates how this works on a simplified GPU with six SMs and eight threads per SM, giving 48 threads in total. Imagine the weights as a long row of empty boxes, wrapped into a grid to fit on the page. The first thread fills the first box, the second fills the second box, and so on through all 48 threads. The first thread’s next number then goes into box 49, its next into box 97, and so forth. The black outlines follow this one thread through the grid: the first thread fills every 48th position. The colors identify which processing unit supplies each set of values, while the brightness in the right-hand panel represents the value itself. Figure 1. How a GPU fills the weights. This simplified example uses six processing units and eight threads per unit, for 48 threads in total. The outlined cells belong to thread 0, which fills every 48th position. Real chips use many more threads, but the placement rule is the same. Link ↗ Now keep the seed fixed, but use a GPU with five SMs instead of six. In our simplified example, that means 40 threads rather than 48. The first thread generates exactly the same sequence, but now puts its numbers in boxes 1, 41, 81, and so on, rather than boxes 1, 49, 97. Figure 2 follows these numbers as their positions change. Across the grid, only 6 percent of the values match the original arrangement. The seed is right, but the worker count is wrong. That is what makes the arrangement of model weights a clue to the chip used to create it. Figure 2. The same seed on a different GPU. With five processing units and 40 threads in this toy example, thread 0 generates the same sequence but fills every 40th position instead of every 48th. Only 6% of the displayed matrix matches the original arrangement. Link ↗ Reproducing the weights therefore requires two things to be right at once. The seed must generate the right numbers, and the thread count must put them in the right places. A correct seed with the wrong thread count mostly gives the right numbers in the wrong positions; a correct thread count with the wrong seed gives different numbers. Figure 3 shows why only the correct combination recreates the original arrangement. Figure 3. Both the seed and the layout must match. The original matrix is reproduced only when the seed and thread count are both correct. Changing either one destroys most of the match. The simplified chips represent a Blackwell B300 and a Hopper H100. Faded cells differ from the published weights. The numbered cells show where thread 0’s numbers land, and the strip beneath each panel shows the numbers themselves. Link ↗ On real chips, the thread counts are much larger, but the principle is the same. In the NVIDIA configurations examined here, the Hopper H100 SXM, H200 and H800 have 132 SMs and use 270,336 threads; the Blackwell B200/B300 have 148 SMs and use 303,104 threads; and the Blackwell GB200/GB300 have 152 SMs and use 311,296 threads. Recovering the thread count therefore tells us which of these hardware groups matches the starting arrangement, although it cannot distinguish chips within a group. A Hopper match, for example, cannot tell an H800 from an H100 or H200. The question is whether enough of that arrangement survives training for us to recover it. Some weights, such as those reserved for words or symbols never encountered during training, can remain untouched and retain their starting values almost exactly. We can compare these preserved values directly with the starting values generated by a candidate seed and thread count. Figure 4 shows such a comparison: DeepSeek-V3’s preserved weights match the Hopper arrangement, while DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s match the Blackwell arrangement. Figure 4. Preserved starting values reveal the layout. Each dot compares a published weight with the value regenerated from the seed. A diagonal line means the values match. DeepSeek-V3 matches the Hopper layout, while V4-Flash matches the Blackwell layout. The panels show 4,096 values from four preserved rows per model. Link ↗ Even weights that training has changed can retain a faint trace of their starting values. Each final weight is its starting value plus all the adjustments made during training. If those adjustments do not completely cancel or overwhelm the starting differences, some of those differences survive. For example, two weights that begin at 0.2 and 0.8 and each increase by about 0.1 will still be ordered the same way afterward. Real adjustments vary much more, so one weight tells us little. But across hundreds of thousands of weights, we can test whether higher starting values still tend to correspond to higher final values. Figure 5 shows this weak but measurable relationship. It is a finding in these weights, not a property guaranteed to survive every training run. Figure 5. Trained weights retain a weaker trace. The left and middle panels average 745,472 weights per layer across 42 layers of DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Under the Blackwell layout, higher starting values still predict slightly higher final values (r = 0.066, 57 sigma); under Hopper, the relationship disappears. The right panel shows the weaker evidence from individual layers. Link ↗ These surviving traces let us work backward. Suppose, in an invented example using Figure 1’s layout, seed 7 makes the first thread produce 0.2, −0.5 and 0.8. With 48 threads, those values go into positions 1, 49 and 97; with 40 threads, they go into positions 1, 41 and 81. If the published weights preserve the first pattern, we can try candidate seeds and thread counts until we recreate it. In the actual investigation, we compare thousands of values in their corresponding positions. Untouched weights can match exactly; trained weights may show only the weaker resemblance described above. In either case, we look for the combination that best reproduces the surviving pattern. We then test that combination on weights we kept out of the search. Having chosen a seed and thread count using one set of weights, we use them to predict the starting values of a different set, without changing either setting to improve the fit. A match on these previously unused weights is stronger evidence than a match confined to the weights that helped us choose the combination. Link ↗ In our investigations, we found patterns strongly suggestive of initialization on Blackwell chips in six models from four Chinese companies: DeepSeek-V4-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Pro from DeepSeek, Kimi K3 and Kimi K3.1-Pro from Moonshot AI, MiniMax-M3 from MiniMax, and Ling-3.1-flash from Ant Group. V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 match the 148-SM layout; the other four match the 152-SM layout. These are fingerprints of the starting weights, which support, but do not by themselves prove, the use of Blackwell chips for training AI models. Limits of our investigation Notably, the forensic method we used to identify the hardware on which these models were initialized only works for certain models. It needs published weights, so closed models cannot be checked. It also needs a recognizable, hardware-dependent pattern from the software that generated the starting weights. PyTorch on the GPUs examined here leaves such a pattern; Baidu’s PaddlePaddle framework, which was used to train Baidu’s ERNIE-5.5 model, does not. We were able to recover the seed for ERNIE-5.5 (2760), but could not identify which hardware was used to initialize it. Likewise, weights initialized on an ordinary processor rather than a GPU leave no GPU fingerprint; several of Alibaba’s Qwen3 models were initialized this way, and thus leave no trace of which GPUs were used to train them. We also found no fingerprint in Meituan’s LongCat-2.0, which the company says was trained on “AI ASIC superpods,” or in DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, despite an exhaustive search. The method identifies the hardware that generated the starting weights, not every chip that later helped train the model. When a training run creates its weights on the same GPUs that will train it, the fingerprint points to both. But a lab could generate the weights on one system and move them to another, or continue training an existing model on new hardware. The weights alone cannot rule out those possibilities. A mixed cluster introduces the same limitation. If NVIDIA chips generated some weights and Huawei chips later helped train them, the NVIDIA pattern could survive without revealing Huawei’s participation. Different NVIDIA generations could leave different patterns in the parts they initialized, if those traces survived. In Kimi K3, at least 64 separately seeded processes each left the same 152-SM layout. A Blackwell-compatible pattern therefore supports its use at initialization, subject to the AMD alternative below; it does not establish that the entire training run used Blackwell. A Hopper pattern likewise does not rule out later training on Blackwell. The weights also cannot reveal who owned the chips or where they were located. Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. The evidence concerns access to the hardware; by itself, it does not establish that chips were smuggled into China or that an export-control violation occurred. Could a different chip produce one of these Blackwell-compatible patterns? Among the NVIDIA configurations tested here, the older chips cannot: software can use fewer of a chip’s processing units, but cannot give it more than it physically has. Under the standard PyTorch behavior examined here, they cannot produce the 148- or 152-SM layouts. The China-market Blackwell graphics cards use a different number of threads per SM and do not produce either total. AMD presents a different possibility. An MI300X normally uses 304 processing units, but it can be divided into two groups of 152 or configured to use only 148. Its random-number software can also generate the same underlying sequences as NVIDIA’s. Such configurations would be very unusual, but we confirmed on a physical MI300X that, limited to 152 or 148 of its units, it reproduces the layouts we associate with Blackwell, so the layout alone does not settle the question. To distinguish them, we looked for small numerical differences in the values themselves. AMD and NVIDIA perform one calculation in the number-generating process slightly differently. On a physical MI300X, DeepSeek-V4-Flash’s preserved weights point to NVIDIA: in the 377 values where the two vendors’ results differ, the published weight matches NVIDIA’s in 363 and AMD’s in none. The same test could not settle the other five models, but we consider the AMD explanation very unlikely for them. In its normal configuration, an MI300X produces neither layout; a lab would have had to configure an entire cluster to use the same number of processing units as a Blackwell chip. Other public evidence also points to Blackwell: U.S. officials and press reports have alleged that DeepSeek and Moonshot AI were using Blackwell chips, and Ant Group’s public code includes benchmark results generated on a GB300. Verifying our findings To reproduce the result that linked DeepSeek-V3 to Hopper and DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Blackwell, we ran unmodified PyTorch on a Hopper-class NVIDIA H100 and a Blackwell-class NVIDIA B300. We had identified DeepSeek’s seed number as 953049583, and found that it was used in the initialization of both DeepSeek-V3 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Using that seed, the H100 reproduced the preserved starting values in DeepSeek-V3, but not V4-Flash; the B300 reproduced the preserved values in V4-Flash, but not V3. On the B300, unmodified PyTorch reproduced 461 of the 469 selected rows in DeepSeek-V4-Flash with correlations above 0.99, including 445 entire rows that matched bit for bit. Eight selected rows were partly changed by training. On the H100, it reproduced all 57,344 preserved values in DeepSeek-V3 bit for bit. Neither chip reproduced the other model’s preserved rows. Changing the seed by one reproduced no matching rows on either machine. On a rented GB200, unmodified PyTorch likewise reproduced all 13 of Kimi K3’s preserved rows using Moonshot’s seed, 20256586; changing the seed by one reproduced none. The code and the preserved weights needed to repeat these checks are public ; the same comparison also runs without a GPU. Our forensic method also gets the right answer when the answer is already known. There are 24 cases where a developer has publicly named the hardware behind a specific model; our forensic method agrees with every one. Meta’s Llama 3.1 models, trained on H100s, read as 132; eight of EleutherAI’s Pythia models, trained on A100s, read as 108. NVIDIA’s own Nemotron-3 Ultra, whose technical report names the GB200 for one phase of training, reads as 152, the same as Kimi K3. DeepSeek and Moonshot have reported H800 use for earlier models. Our Hopper readings are consistent with those disclosures, but would also be consistent with H100 SXM or H200 hardware; they do not independently verify H800 use. When we compare the published weights with the numbers generated by a candidate seed and chip layout, some resemblance is inevitable even if the candidate is wrong. How much resemblance counts as evidence depends on how many weights we compare: agreement across a handful of numbers could easily be accidental, while agreement across thousands is much harder to explain by chance. Our statistical model accounts for the number of weights compared and measures how far the observed match exceeds the resemblance expected by chance. We express that distance in standard deviations, or sigma . A higher score means stronger evidence against an accidental match, provided the statistical model correctly describes the random variation in the data. We must also account for how many candidates we tried. Searching roughly six trillion combinations of seed and layout gives us trillions of opportunities to find a lucky match. Under a normal-distribution model, a positive match of five sigma or more occurs by chance about once in 3.5 million comparisons. That would be striking in a single test, but unsurprising somewhere in a search as large as ours. We therefore use approximately eight sigma as our benchmark for assessing accidental matches across the full search. Our findings exceed that benchmark by a wide margin. We first select a seed and layout using one set of weights, and then test that same combination on a separate set that played no part in choosing it. This checks whether the apparent fingerprint extends beyond the numbers that led us to it. The strongest evidence for each of the six models ranges from 49 to 1,385 sigma; even the weakest individual test reported reaches 20 sigma. Under our statistical model, these results are far too strong to attribute to accidental resemblance. They establish evidence of a shared initialization pattern; identifying precisely which computing hardware produced that pattern, and whether it also performed the training, requires the separate arguments discussed above. Conclusion Based on our forensic investigation, we believe that we have strong evidence that six Chinese AI models were initialized on export-controlled NVIDIA hardware, and that for DeepSeek-V4-Flash the evidence is conclusive ; we believe that this initialization also strongly suggests that they trained on the same export-controlled hardware. While this leaves unanswered other questions—such as the circumstances through which the companies that developed these models acquired export-controlled NVIDIA systems—we believe that this fact deserves urgent attention from the public.
